title: A happy place: how our words and actions change how other people feel and act

summary.text: Drop 15 chana into a bottle, one at a time, and you may miss twice. Do it again while someone counts down and says 'faster', and many people miss more often. The chana, the bottle and the hand are the same. Another person's words set off the body's stress response, and tight, hurried hands aim badly. Feelings and actions pass between people all the time. A smile is returned, a push is copied, and one wrapper on the ground leads to more. So the people who use a place make it happy or unhappy, by what they do there every day. Your child tests this, finds the barriers in their own home, and practises kind and safe ways to step in.
summary.art: A child's hand dropping a chana towards the mouth of a plastic bottle that stands on a steel plate, while a second child beside her counts down on her fingers.

intro.hook: When someone counts down and says 'faster', a hand can miss the bottle more often. Why would another person's words change what your hand can do?
intro.text: Most people think a skill belongs to one person. She is careful, or he is clumsy. But the same child reads aloud well at home and stumbles when classmates laugh. The same lane stays clean for months and then fills with litter in a week. In this unit you find out how words, faces and actions pass from one person to the next. You run the Hurry Test on your own hands. You measure your doors as a wheelchair user would. You learn what to do when you see teasing or pushing. Then you can say what makes a school, a home or a street a happy place, and what your part in it is.
intro.art: Two pictures side by side of the same girl reading aloud from a book: calm and smiling beside one friendly listener, and stiff with a red face in front of three laughing children.

outcomes: I can say what makes a place happy: people are safe there, belong there, and care for the place.
I can explain how feelings and actions pass from one person to another.
I can run a fair test of how hurrying words change a person's hands, and say what the result shows.
I can explain what respect is, and why every honest job deserves it.
I can describe a day from another person's point of view, and find the barriers in a place.
I can choose a kind and safe action when I see teasing, pushing or damage, and say when to tell a trusted grown-up.
I can explain why a cared-for place stays cared for, and why one mess leads to more.
I can name things that calm a big feeling, and I know to tell a trusted grown-up when a feeling is too big.

terms.meaning: Being well in body, in feelings and with other people, all together.
terms.example: A child who sleeps enough, has friends to talk to and is safe at school has good well-being.
terms.art: A child stretching happily in the morning beside a window, with a friend waving from the door.

terms.meaning: A feeling, such as joy, fear or anger, that happens in the body and the mind together.
terms.example: Before a race your heart beats fast and your tummy feels tight. That emotion is excitement or fear.
terms.art: A child at a starting line with a hand on her chest and wide eyes.

terms.meaning: The passing of a feeling from one person to another, mostly without either one choosing it. Contagion means spreading.
terms.example: One child starts to giggle in class, and soon the whole row is giggling.
terms.art: A row of five children on a bench, with a giggle shown passing from the first to the last.

terms.meaning: The body getting ready for action when something seems urgent or unsafe. The heart speeds up and the muscles tighten.
terms.example: When someone shouts 'faster!', your heart beats quicker and your fingers tighten.
terms.art: An outline of a child's body with the heart, the lungs and the arm muscles marked in a warm colour.

terms.meaning: A substance that two small glands above the kidneys release into the blood. It makes the heart beat faster within seconds.
terms.example: A sudden loud bang sends adrenaline into your blood, and your heart thumps.
terms.art: An outline of a body showing two small glands sitting on top of the kidneys, with arrows to the heart.

terms.meaning: What most people in a place do, or what they think they should do there.
terms.example: At a temple, mosque or gurdwara door, everyone takes off their shoes. A visitor sees this and does the same.
terms.art: A row of chappals and shoes outside a doorway, and a new visitor bending to take off her sandals.

terms.meaning: Actions that make things better for the people and the place around you.
terms.example: Waiting for your turn, putting a book back and helping a younger child are positive behaviour.
terms.art: A child putting a book back on a shelf while another child holds the chair steady.

terms.meaning: Treating a person as someone who matters as much as you do.
terms.example: You listen until a classmate finishes speaking, though you disagree.
terms.art: Two children facing each other, one speaking and one listening with her hands in her lap.

terms.meaning: Feeling some of what another person feels, and caring about it.
terms.example: Your friend drops her tiffin, and you feel a pang as if the tiffin were yours.
terms.art: A girl kneeling to help another girl pick up a spilled tiffin box.

terms.meaning: What a person sees, knows, needs and feels from where they are.
terms.example: From a wheelchair, three steps at a doorway are a wall.
terms.art: The same doorway drawn twice: seen from standing height, and seen from the height of a seated person facing three steps.

terms.meaning: Anything in a place that stops some people from using it.
terms.example: A step with no ramp, a switch too high to reach and a notice in only one language are barriers.
terms.art: A doorway with one step, a high light switch and a notice board, each marked with a small cross.

terms.meaning: Built so that everyone can get in and use it, whatever their body can do.
terms.example: A toilet with a wide door, a ramp and a handrail is accessible.
terms.art: A wide doorway with a gentle ramp and a handrail, and a child in a wheelchair rolling through.

terms.meaning: Changing a place, and the way we act, so that every person can take part.
terms.example: The class learns five signs so that a deaf classmate can join the game.
terms.art: A circle of children playing a clapping game, one of them signing with her hands.

terms.meaning: The idea that every honest job deserves equal respect.
terms.example: The person who cleans the school toilets is greeted by name, like the teachers.
terms.art: A child greeting a sanitation worker who holds a broom, both of them smiling.

terms.meaning: Hurting, frightening or leaving out the same person again and again, when that person finds it hard to make it stop.
terms.example: Three children hide one boy's bag every day and laugh when he looks for it.
terms.art: A boy searching under a bench for his school bag while three children watch from behind a pillar.

terms.meaning: A person who sees something happen and is not the one doing it or the one it is done to.
terms.example: The children standing around when someone is teased are bystanders.
terms.art: A ring of children standing around two others in a playground, some looking away.

terms.meaning: An adult you know well, who listens to you and keeps you safe.
terms.example: A parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a teacher or a school counsellor can be a trusted grown-up.
terms.art: A child sitting beside a woman on a step, talking, while the woman listens with her full attention.

terms.meaning: A place that many people use and that no single person owns.
terms.example: The stairs of a building, a classroom, a playground and a bus stop are shared places.
terms.art: The staircase of a block of flats with shoes, a bicycle and plant pots belonging to different homes.

terms.meaning: A short list of rules that the people of a place agree on together and sign.
terms.example: A family writes five rules for their study corner, and everyone signs the page.
terms.art: A sheet of paper titled with five short lines and four signatures at the bottom, pinned to a wall.

explanations.definition: A happy place is one where people are safe, belong, and can do what they came to do. The people in it, and the way they treat each other, matter most.
explanations.description: Well-being means that a person's body, feelings and friendships are all doing well. A place can add to well-being or take away from it. Four things decide which. The first is safety: nobody is hurt, pushed or frightened there. The second is belonging: everyone is greeted, gets a turn and can take part. The third is care for the place: the room is clean, the water runs, and broken things get fixed. The fourth is something worth doing there, such as learning, playing or working. In Three Good Places, you sort your own reasons into people and things. Most children find that people come first. A new building full of unkind people is an unhappy place. A plain room with kind people is often a happy one. So the people who use a place make most of what it is like, and they make it again every day.
examples: A school where older children help the youngest find their classroom on the first day.
A building where neighbours greet each other on the stairs and keep the landing clear.
A playground where the swings are mended in the same week that they break.
A classroom where a wrong answer is met with 'good try', and nobody laughs.
explanations.art: A school courtyard with a neem tree, children washing hands in a line at a row of taps, and a teacher greeting a child at the gate.

explanations.concept: Feelings pass from person to person
explanations.definition: Emotional contagion is the passing of a feeling from one person to another, mostly without either one choosing it.
explanations.description: When you watch a face, the small muscles of your own face begin to copy it. In 2000 the scientist Ulf Dimberg and his team measured this with sensors on people's cheeks and brows. The muscles moved within half a second. They moved even when the face was shown too briefly to notice. Your voice and the way you stand copy the people near you too. Your brain reads your own face and body, and takes the copied look for a feeling of your own. So one cheerful person can lift a whole room, and one cross voice can spoil it. The psychologist Elaine Hatfield and her colleagues named this emotional contagion in the early 1990s. In the Smile Count, you find out how often a smile is returned, and how often a plain face is. Each face in a room is partly made by the other faces in it.
examples: A baby in a clinic starts to cry, and the other babies start crying too.
A cricket crowd groans together when a catch is dropped.
In the Smile Count, you count how many smiles come back after a smile, and after a plain face.
A teacher who comes in calm and smiling gets a calmer class.
explanations.art: Two faces looking at each other, with thin lines showing the cheek muscles of the second face beginning to lift like the first.

explanations.concept: People copy what they see others do
explanations.definition: A social norm is what most people in a place do. People follow what they see being done more than what they are told to do.
explanations.description: A person in a new place looks around to find out what is done there. In 2008 Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg and Linda Steg tested this in an alley in Groningen, in the Netherlands, where people parked bicycles. The scientists hung a paper advert on every handlebar. There was no bin. When the walls were clean, 33 of every 100 riders dropped the paper on the ground. When the walls were covered in scribbles, 69 of every 100 dropped it. Nobody had told the riders anything. The walls had told them that people here break rules. Words can even work backwards. A park in the United States put up a sign saying that many visitors stole pieces of its ancient stone wood. Theft went up. So a wrapper on the ground is a message: people drop wrappers here. A line at a tap is a message too: people wait here. Younger children read these messages from older children. Everything you do in a shared place tells the next person what is done there.
examples: Passengers stand in a line for the bus in some cities and crowd the door in others.
A small child who sees big children push at the water tap begins to push.
One pair of shoes left on the stairs is soon joined by three more.
When three people start to clap, a whole hall claps.
explanations.art: An alley with bicycles parked along a wall, shown twice: with a clean wall and no paper on the ground, and with a scribbled wall and paper scattered below.

explanations.concept: How one person's words change another person's body
explanations.definition: The stress response is the body getting ready for action when something seems urgent or unsafe. Another person's words can start it.
explanations.description: When someone shouts 'faster!' or laughs at you, your brain treats the moment as urgent. Within a second or two, nerves signal the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys. They release adrenaline into the blood. The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, and the muscles tighten, ready to run or push. This helps in a race. It harms careful work. Tight muscles shake a little, and a hurried brain spends less time on aiming. In the Hurry Test, many people miss the bottle more often in the hurried runs, and say their body felt tighter. Teasing does the same to a child who is reading aloud, catching a ball or answering in class. Calm and friendly words do the opposite. The body stays loose, and the person can use all the skill they have. So the people around you are part of how well you do, and you are part of how well they do.
examples: A child who knows the answer forgets it when the class turns to stare.
A bowler bowls a wide after the fielders jeer at her run-up.
In the made-up results of the Hurry Test, the hurried runs had three times as many misses.
A learner threads a needle more easily when the teacher says 'take your time'.
explanations.art: A child's hand above a bottle, drawn twice: steady with a loose wrist, and tense with small shake lines around the fingers and a quick heartbeat line above.

explanations.concept: Respect, and the dignity of labour
explanations.definition: Respect means treating a person as someone who matters as much as you do. Dignity of labour means that every honest job deserves equal respect.
explanations.description: Respect shows in small acts. You greet people, listen without cutting in, wait for your turn and ask before you touch someone's things. You use a person's name. Respect is owed to everyone, whatever their age, language, body, religion, caste, money or work. Yet some work is treated as low, although no place can run without it. A school with no sanitation workers would be unfit to use within days, and illness would spread. The people who do this work are often not greeted and not named. In India this work was forced on particular castes for centuries, and that injustice has not ended. Bezwada Wilson, who grew up in Karnataka, has campaigned for decades to end the cleaning of dry toilets by hand. He won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2016. Respect for work is also practical. Learn the worker's name. Make their work easier and safer: wrap broken glass, and keep wet and dry waste apart.
examples: Children greet the school's sanitation worker by name each morning.
A family wraps a broken tumbler in newspaper and writes GLASS on it for the waste collector.
A class thanks the cook after the noon meal.
A child offers water to the worker who repairs the lift.
explanations.art: A woman in a sanitation worker's uniform and gloves collecting two separate bins, while a child hands her a wrapped parcel marked GLASS.

explanations.concept: Seeing a place from another person's point of view
explanations.definition: Taking someone's point of view means working out what they see, know and need from where they are. Inclusion means changing a place so that everyone can take part.
explanations.description: Your own point of view comes without effort. Another person's takes work, and people often skip that work. In The E on Your Forehead, many people draw the letter so that only they can read it. Places get built the same way. People who walk easily build steps, narrow doors and high switches. For a person who uses a wheelchair, each of these is a barrier. A common wheelchair is about 65 centimetres wide, and a door should be at least 90 centimetres wide for it to pass easily. One step of 15 centimetres stops a wheelchair. A safe ramp needs 12 centimetres of length for every centimetre of height, so that step needs a ramp 180 centimetres long. Language can be a barrier too. In Lost for Words, an instruction in an unknown language does not get clearer when it is said louder. Pointing and showing work. A change made for one person usually helps many. A ramp also helps a grandparent, a parent with a pram and a worker with a trolley.
examples: A ramp beside the steps of a railway station, used by wheelchairs, trolleys and suitcases.
A lift button low enough for a seated person and a small child.
A teacher who shows each step with her hands for a child new to the language.
Raised dots in Braille beside the numbers in a lift.
explanations.art: A building entrance with three steps and a long gentle ramp beside them, used by a girl in a wheelchair, a man with a trolley and a grandmother with a stick.

explanations.concept: Teasing, bullying and the children who watch
explanations.definition: Bullying is hurting, frightening or leaving out the same person again and again, when that person finds it hard to make it stop. Friendly teasing is fun for both sides and stops when one side says stop.
explanations.description: Bullying is rarely a matter between two children. Films of school playgrounds in Toronto showed other children present in more than eight of every ten bullying episodes. Watchers give the bullying an audience, and laughing along joins it. The same films showed that when one child stepped in, the bullying stopped within 10 seconds more than half the time. Stepping in must be kind and safe. There are four ways. Say it calmly: 'Stop. That is not funny.' Stand beside the person, and take them away to play with you. Put right what you can yourself. Tell a trusted grown-up. Telling to get someone out of trouble is different from telling tales, which is done to get someone into trouble. Always tell a grown-up when someone is being hurt or threatened, or when the unkindness keeps happening. If it is happening to you, it is not your fault. Telling is the right thing to do, and you can keep telling until someone listens.
examples: A girl says 'come and play with us' to a classmate whose name others are making fun of.
Two children refuse to laugh at a joke about a boy's stammer, and the joke falls flat.
A child tells her teacher that a younger boy's lunch is taken from him every day.
Two friends tease each other about a missed goal, and both are laughing.
explanations.art: A playground where one girl has stepped out of a ring of watching children to stand beside a boy who is being teased, her hand held out to him.

explanations.concept: Why a cared-for place stays cared for
explanations.definition: A shared place belongs to everyone who uses it. Signs of care lead to more care, and signs of mess lead to more mess.
explanations.description: In the game Keep the Lane Clean, a passer-by copies the wrappers already lying in the lane. With 2 wrappers there, one passer-by in three adds another. With 4 wrappers, two in three add another. So a mess feeds itself, and the first wrapper matters most. Picking it up early costs one small act. Leaving it costs many acts later. The same holds for a scribble on a bench, a dripping tap and shoes left on the stairs. There are three ways to care for a shared place. Do your own part: use the bin, turn the tap off and put things back. Repair early: pick up the first wrapper, and report the drip on the day you see it. Make the right action easy to see and easy to do: a bin close by, a line to join, a sign that says what most people here do. Rules last longest when the people who use the place agree on them together.
examples: A classroom where the first torn poster is taped up the same day, and the walls stay neat all year.
A staircase where one family's bag of rubbish is soon joined by others.
A railway platform that stays clean after bins are placed every twenty steps.
In Keep the Lane Clean, a lane that starts with 4 wrappers is much harder to save than a lane that starts with 2.
explanations.art: A lane between houses drawn twice: swept, with one child putting a wrapper in a bin, and littered, with a passer-by letting a wrapper fall.

explanations.concept: Calming a big feeling, and asking for help
explanations.definition: A big feeling is a strong stress response. It settles sooner when you breathe out slowly, name the feeling, move your body or talk to someone you trust.
explanations.description: The body clears adrenaline from the blood within a few minutes, if nothing sets off more. Going over the upsetting thought again and again sets off more. Four things help the body settle. Breathe out slowly, for longer than you breathe in. The heart slows a little on every out-breath. Name the feeling exactly: 'I am embarrassed' says more than 'I feel bad'. Move: walk, stretch or wash your face. Talk to a person you trust. What works best differs from person to person, and the log called What Helped? shows what works for you. Every feeling is allowed. Hurting someone because of a feeling is not. Some feelings are too big to carry alone. A worry or a sadness may stay for many days. A secret may frighten you. Someone may be hurting you. When something feels too big, tell a trusted grown-up, and keep telling until one of them listens. People of every age ask for help, and it is a sensible thing to do.
examples: A child who lost a match takes ten slow out-breaths before shaking hands.
A girl tells her aunt, 'I feel left out', and the two of them plan what to do.
A boy who is angry with his brother walks round the building once before he speaks.
A child tells her teacher about a worry that has kept her awake for a week.
explanations.art: A child sitting on a step breathing out slowly with eyes closed, and the same child a moment later talking to a woman who sits beside her.

explanations.concept: Other animals comfort and help each other
explanations.definition: Helping and comforting are found in many kinds of animals, including humans.
explanations.description: Humans are one helping animal among many. In 2011 Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal, Jean Decety and Peggy Mason put pairs of rats in a box. One rat was shut in a small clear tube, and the other was free. The free rats learned to open the tube and let their companions out. They did this even when a second tube held chocolate. Many of them opened both tubes and shared the chocolate. In 2014 Joshua Plotnik and Frans de Waal watched Asian elephants in Thailand. When one elephant was upset, others came to stand close. They touched the upset elephant with their trunks and made soft chirping calls. Chimpanzees put an arm round a companion who has lost a fight. So comforting others is far older than schools, rules or words. Scientists still disagree about exactly what the helper feels.
examples: A free rat opens a tube to let out a trapped companion.
An elephant strokes an upset elephant with her trunk.
A chimpanzee hugs a companion who has just lost a fight.
A dog comes and sits against a person who is crying.
explanations.art: Two Asian elephants standing close together in a forest clearing, one resting her trunk gently against the other's face.

explanations.concept: Are we born kind, or do we learn to be kind?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that very young children help others. They do not agree on how much of human kindness is inborn and how much is taught.
explanations.description: Three kinds of evidence point in different directions. Toddlers help before anyone has taught them to. Yet people everywhere also look after themselves first, and need rules. And children grow up to share in the way their own community shares.
examples: A toddler of 18 months picks up a peg that a stranger dropped and hands it back.
Children in different societies share differently from about the age of seven.

perspectives.who: Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello, psychologists in Germany, in 2006
perspectives.explanation: They let a grown-up drop a peg or bump into a cupboard in front of toddlers of 18 months. Most toddlers helped within seconds, with no reward and no asking. Young chimpanzees helped in some of the tasks too. So helping begins before teaching.

perspectives.who: Thomas Hobbes, an English philosopher, in his book Leviathan in 1651
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that people look after themselves first. Without rules and someone to enforce them, he said, people would fight over what they want. On this view kindness has to be taught and protected by rules.

perspectives.who: Bailey House and a team of scientists, in 2013
perspectives.explanation: They tested children in six societies, from cities to small forest villages. Young children shared in much the same way everywhere. From about the age of seven, children began to share the way the grown-ups of their own society shared. So a community shapes the kindness a child is born with.

explanations.art: A toddler holding up a clothes peg to a grown-up whose hands are full of washing.

agreed.text: Feelings pass between people through faces, voices and bodies.
agreed.evidence: In 2000 Ulf Dimberg's team recorded the face muscles of people looking at happy and angry faces. Their own muscles copied the faces within half a second, even when the faces were shown too briefly to notice.

agreed.text: People break a rule more often in a place where they see that others have broken rules.
agreed.evidence: In Groningen in 2008, 33 of every 100 bicycle riders dropped a paper advert in a clean alley. In the same alley with scribbled walls, 69 of every 100 did.

agreed.text: Pressure from other people changes the body within minutes: the heart, the breathing and the muscles.
agreed.evidence: Since 1993, scientists have asked volunteers to give a speech and do sums in front of silent judges. Heart rate and stress hormones rise in most people.

agreed.text: Other children are present at most bullying, and one child who steps in often stops it.
agreed.evidence: Lynn Hawkins, Debra Pepler and Wendy Craig studied films of playgrounds in Toronto, published in 2001. When a child stepped in, the bullying stopped within 10 seconds in 57 of every 100 cases.

agreed.text: Talk in the background makes it harder to remember things in order, even when you try to ignore it.
agreed.evidence: In 1982 Pierre Salamé and Alan Baddeley asked people to remember lists of digits. They remembered fewer when speech was played, even speech in a language they did not know.

agreed.text: Very young children help other people without being asked and without a reward.
agreed.evidence: In 2006 Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello tested toddlers of 18 months. Most of them picked up dropped things and opened cupboards for a grown-up they had only just met.

challenging.claim: Children who only watch bullying are not part of it.
challenging.for: The watchers did not start it, and they said nothing unkind.
challenging.against: Films of playgrounds in Toronto showed watchers at more than eight of every ten episodes. An audience keeps bullying going. When one watcher stepped in, it stopped within 10 seconds more than half the time.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about the children who stand and watch bullying, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: When many people are watching, nobody helps.
challenging.who: John Darley and Bibb Latané in 1968, and many textbooks since.
challenging.for: In their test, a person heard someone fall ill over an intercom. Of those who thought they were the only listener, 85 in 100 went for help. Of those who thought four others could hear, 31 in 100 did.
challenging.against: In 2020 Richard Philpot's team studied street cameras in Amsterdam, Lancaster and Cape Town. They watched 219 real quarrels. In 9 of every 10, at least one bystander stepped in, and more bystanders made help more likely.
challenging.context: This is a famous idea about crowds. Scientists now argue about how well it fits real life.

challenging.claim: Telling people how many others break a rule will make them stop.
challenging.who: Many notice boards and signs are written as if this were true.
challenging.for: It shows that the problem is serious.
challenging.against: Robert Cialdini's team tested signs in the Petrified Forest park in Arizona. A sign saying that many visitors took the ancient stone wood led to more theft: about 8 of every 100 marked pieces. A sign that simply asked visitors not to take wood led to fewer than 2 in 100.
challenging.context: This is an idea behind many warning signs, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.for: Friendly teasing between equals is a kind of play, and it can bring friends closer.
challenging.against: Teasing that the other person does not enjoy sets off the stress response. In the Hurry Test, a countdown can make hands miss more often. Children who are bullied again and again enjoy school less and do worse at their work.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about teasing, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Cleaning is unskilled work, so it deserves less respect.
challenging.for: The work needs no degree, and it is often poorly paid.
challenging.against: A cleaner must know how to handle sharp and infected waste, and which chemicals must never be mixed. The work stops disease for everyone else. How long a person studied for a job does not measure how much others depend on it.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about cleaning work, with the reasons for it and against it.

challenging.who: Some philosophers and some biologists say this.
challenging.for: Helpers often get help back later, and helping feels good to the helper.
challenging.against: Toddlers and rats help with no reward in sight. People return lost purses to strangers they will never meet. A good feeling afterwards does not show that the feeling was the aim.
challenging.context: This is an old argument about why anyone helps anyone else.

big_questions.q: In the Hurry Test, the same hand did worse when someone hurried it. So does a skill belong to one person, or to the people in the room together?
big_questions.hint: Think about who changed between the calm runs and the hurried runs, and what stayed the same.

big_questions.q: A new child copies what they see, whether it is pushing or a line. Who decides what is normal in a place?
big_questions.hint: Think about the first three people at a tap, and about the hundredth.

big_questions.q: A place can teach a rule without any words. How does a clean wall or a scribbled wall tell you what to do?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you look at first when you enter a place you have never been to.

big_questions.q: The work that no place can run without is often paid and respected the least. Is that fair, and why does it happen?
big_questions.hint: Think about who does this work, who decides the pay, and what would happen in a week if the work stopped.

big_questions.q: A ramp built for one wheelchair user also helps many other people. Should every place be designed for the person who finds it hardest?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cost, about who benefits, and about who is left out when nothing changes.

big_questions.q: A rat frees a trapped companion and shares her chocolate. Did humans invent kindness, or is it older than humans?
big_questions.hint: Think about elephants, chimpanzees and toddlers, none of whom were taught a rule about helping.

story.title: Three in a Line
story.note: Thenmozhi, Sasmita, Kavin, Poongodi, Fathima, Yamuna teacher, Rajathi akka and the school are made up. These facts are real. Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu is a town of knitwear factories, and many families from Odisha and other states work there. Schools in Tamil Nadu serve a free noon meal. 'Thanni' is the everyday Tamil word for water, and 'pani' is the Odia word. Tests by scientists show that people copy what they see others doing more than what they are told.
text: At Thenmozhi's school in Tiruppur, lunch began at the taps. A long pipe ran behind the kitchen, with six taps on it. Every child had to wash there before Rajathi akka would fill a plate.

Nobody stood in a line. Two hundred children came round the corner in a bunch and pushed in from the sides. The small ones were squeezed to the back. Water ran on to the ground while people argued, and by one o'clock the mud was ankle-deep.
In June, Yamuna teacher made Thenmozhi the tap monitor. Thenmozhi was in Class 5, and she had the loudest voice in the school. She was sure that was why she had been chosen.

On the first day she stood on the kitchen step and shouted. "One line! One line! Don't push!" A few children looked up. Then the bunch closed again. She shouted louder. By Friday her throat hurt, and the mud was as deep as ever.
"They don't listen," she told Poongodi and Fathima. "I say it fifty times."
"You say it very well," said Fathima. "Nobody can hear anything else."

The new girl came in the second week. Her name was Sasmita. Her mother and father had come from Odisha to work in a knitwear factory, and at home she spoke Odia. She knew about ten words of Tamil. She sat in the front row of Class 4 and watched the teacher's hands.

At lunch Sasmita walked out with her plate, saw the bunch at the taps, and stopped. She stood at the edge for a long time. Then she did what everyone else was doing. She put her shoulder down and pushed in from the side.
"Hey! New girl! LINE!" Thenmozhi shouted from the step.

Sasmita turned round. She looked at Thenmozhi's mouth. Then she looked at the children on both sides of her, who were pushing too. Her face went stiff. She stepped back out of the bunch and stood by the wall, with her hands still dry.
Somebody laughed. "She doesn't even know the word 'line'."

Thenmozhi opened her mouth to shout again, and found that she had nothing to shout. The girl had not understood one word. But she had understood the taps perfectly. She had looked at what two hundred children were doing, and she had done it too.

Thenmozhi looked at the bunch for a while. Perhaps everybody here had learned the taps in the same way. Nobody at this school had ever seen a line. They had only heard about one, from a girl on a step.
That evening she thought about Kavin in Class 2. Last year Kavin used to wait at the back until the taps were free. This year he pushed. Nobody had told him to. He had spent a year watching Class 5.

The next day Thenmozhi did not go up on the step. She asked Poongodi and Fathima to leave class with her two minutes before the bell. They went to the first tap and stood one behind the other, with their plates under their arms.
"This is silly," said Poongodi. "Three people are not a line."
"Stand straight," said Thenmozhi. "And don't say anything."

The bell rang. The bunch came round the corner of the kitchen, loud as always, and went for the taps. Five taps disappeared under elbows. At the first tap, a few children slowed down. Three big girls stood in a row there, and it was not clear how to push past a row.

Sasmita came out last, as she did every day. She stopped at the edge and looked. Thenmozhi kept her eyes on the tap and did not call out. From the corner of her eye she saw the new girl look at the five bunches, and then at the one row. Sasmita walked over and stood behind Fathima.
Now there were four.

Kavin came next. A line has a place at the end, and that is easier for a small boy than a wall of backs. Then came two girls from Class 3. Then came a boy who looked round first, to see if anyone was laughing at him. Nobody was.

When Thenmozhi's turn came, she washed her hands, turned the tap off tightly and stepped aside. Fathima did the same, and so did Sasmita. Thenmozhi had not asked them to. At the other five taps the water was still running on to the ground.
She found Sasmita by the kitchen door afterwards and pointed back at the tap. "Thanni," she said. "Water. Thanni."
"Thanni," said Sasmita. She pointed at the tap too. "Pani."
"Pani," said Thenmozhi. It was the first Odia word she had ever said. Sasmita's face was not stiff any more.
By the next Friday the first tap had a line every day, and the second tap had grown a line that nobody had started on purpose. Yamuna teacher came out to look. "You have stopped shouting," she said.
"Nobody could see what I was shouting," said Thenmozhi.

On Monday she came out two minutes early again. Three children were already standing at the first tap, one behind the other. Kavin was at the front, standing very straight. Thenmozhi walked to the end of the line and stood there.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Thenmozhi thought that children would behave well if she told them loudly enough. Sasmita, who knew no Tamil, showed her the mistake. Sasmita pushed because she saw pushing, and joined a line as soon as she could see a line. People, and new people most of all, learn what is done in a place by watching what others do. So the surest way to change how a place behaves is to do the right thing where others can see it.
ask: Thenmozhi shouted 'one line' for a week. Why did the shouting change nothing?
Sasmita did not know the word 'line'. How did she know what to do on the second day?
Kavin waited last year and pushed this year. What had changed for him?
Is there a place you use where people copy something unhelpful? What could three people do there?

games.title: Kind and Safe: what would you do?
games.context: This is a card game about what to do when you see pushing, teasing, damage or someone left out. Each card describes a situation. You choose one of four actions, and the back of the card tells you the good choices.

printables.title: 4 action cards. Keep them face up in the middle
items: SAY IT CALMLY. Use a steady voice and few words. For example: 'Stop. That is not kind.'
STAND BESIDE. Go and stand or sit with the person. Ask them to come and play or work with you.
PUT IT RIGHT. Do the helpful thing yourself: pick it up, turn it off, start the line, say sorry.
TELL A GROWN-UP. Tell a teacher, a parent or another grown-up you trust. Do this at once if someone is being hurt or threatened.

printables.title: 20 situation cards. The good choices are on the back

items.f: Children push and skip the line at the school water tap. A small child is squeezed to the back.
items.b: Good choices: PUT IT RIGHT or SAY IT CALMLY. Start a line yourself, and let the small child stand ahead of you. People copy a line that they can see.

items.f: A classmate scribbles on a bench with a pen. You are the only one watching.
items.b: Good choice: SAY IT CALMLY. 'Please stop. We all sit here.' If it goes on, tell a grown-up. Saying nothing tells the classmate that nobody minds.

items.f: An older child drops a chips wrapper in the playground. A younger child sees this and drops a wrapper too.
items.b: Good choice: PUT IT RIGHT. Pick up both wrappers and show the younger child the bin. Younger children copy what they see older children do.

items.f: Three children make fun of the way a new boy speaks. He looks at the floor.
items.b: Good choices: STAND BESIDE or SAY IT CALMLY. Stand with him and ask him to play with you. Do not laugh. If it happens again, tell a grown-up.

items.f: Children play loud music in a park, right beside a group doing yoga.
items.b: Good choice: SAY IT CALMLY. Ask your friends to move further away or turn the sound down. A park is shared by everyone in it.

items.f: A bigger child hits a smaller child behind the toilets and says, 'If you tell anyone, you are next.'
items.b: ALWAYS TELL A GROWN-UP, at once. Someone is being hurt and threatened. Do not step in alone. Fetch a teacher or another trusted grown-up.

items.f: Your friend whispers that someone at home hurts her. She asks you to keep it a secret.
items.b: ALWAYS TELL A GROWN-UP you trust. A secret about someone being hurt is too big for a child to keep. Telling is how your friend gets help.

items.f: The class goes up three steps to the library. A girl who uses a wheelchair is left waiting at the bottom.
items.b: Good choices: STAND BESIDE and TELL A GROWN-UP. Wait with her and tell the teacher. The steps are the problem. The class can ask for a ramp, or bring the books down.

items.f: Someone has left a washroom tap running. Nobody is near.
items.b: Good choice: PUT IT RIGHT. Turn the tap off. If it still drips, tell a teacher on the same day.

items.f: In a game, one girl is always picked last. Today nobody picks her at all.
items.b: Good choice: STAND BESIDE. Say, 'Be on my team.' Leaving the same person out again and again is a kind of bullying.

items.f: A classmate reads aloud slowly. Two children start to giggle.
items.b: Good choices: SAY IT CALMLY or STAND BESIDE. Do not join the giggle. Say quietly, 'Let her finish.' Laughter makes reading aloud harder.

items.f: In a class chat group on a phone, someone posts an unkind photo of a classmate. Others add laughing faces.
items.b: Good choice: TELL A GROWN-UP. Do not add to the chat or pass the photo on. Show a parent or a teacher. Things online spread fast and are hard to undo.

items.f: You bump into a child by accident, and their tiffin spills on the floor.
items.b: Good choices: PUT IT RIGHT and SAY IT CALMLY. Say sorry, help to clean up, and share your own food. An accident needs repair more than excuses.

items.f: The sanitation worker is mopping the corridor. Children run across the wet floor in muddy shoes.
items.b: Good choices: PUT IT RIGHT or SAY IT CALMLY. Walk round the wet part, and ask the others to do the same. Greet the worker by name.

items.f: A child from another state has joined your class. She does not know your language yet, and she sits alone at lunch.
items.b: Good choice: STAND BESIDE. Sit with her. Point, show and smile. Learn one word of her language and teach her one of yours.

items.f: Your best friend says, 'Stop talking to that girl, or I will not be your friend.'
items.b: Good choice: SAY IT CALMLY. 'I want to be friends with both of you.' A friend who asks you to leave someone out is asking for something unfair.

items.f: A grown-up you do not know well asks you to keep a secret from your parents.
items.b: ALWAYS TELL A GROWN-UP you trust. Safe grown-ups do not ask children to keep secrets from their parents.

items.f: Someone has written a rude word about a teacher on the classroom wall.
items.b: Good choices: TELL A GROWN-UP or PUT IT RIGHT. Tell a teacher, so that the wall is cleaned today. Marks on a wall invite more marks.

items.f: A classmate takes your pencil without asking. You are so angry that you want to push him.
items.b: Good choice: SAY IT CALMLY, after three slow out-breaths. 'I am angry, because you took my pencil without asking.' Every feeling is allowed. Pushing is not.

items.f: An old neighbour is climbing the stairs slowly with two heavy bags.
items.b: Good choice: PUT IT RIGHT. Ask first: 'May I carry one?' Asking shows respect, because some people like to manage alone.

rules: Put the 4 action cards face up in the middle. Shuffle the 20 situation cards and stack them with the situations facing up.
On your turn, take the top card. Read the situation aloud, and do not turn the card over yet.
Point to the action card you would choose. Say the exact words you would say, or exactly what you would do.
Now turn the card over and read the back aloud. If your action is one of the good choices, keep the card.
If your action is not on the back, put the card at the bottom of the stack. It will come round again.
The game ends when the stack is gone, or after 15 minutes. The player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone? Lay the 4 action cards in a row. Sort all 20 situations under them. Then turn the cards over, and count how many you matched.

setup.art: Four large paper cards face up in the middle of a table, and a stack of twenty smaller cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the 4 action cards in the middle. Stack the 20 situation cards beside them.

setup.art: A child holding one card and reading it aloud while pointing at one of the four action cards.
setup.caption: 2. Read a situation aloud. Point to the action you would choose, and say your exact words.

setup.art: The same child turning the card over to read the back, with a small pile of won cards beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. If your action is a good choice, keep the card.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Read the four action cards aloud together. Ask your child for one example of each action.
flow.say: There are four ways to step in. Give me one example of each, from school, home or the street.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the four actions. Think of an example of each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kind and Safe. You learn the four actions before you play.

flow.do: Play by the rules for 12 minutes. Each time a card is turned over, ask the question below.
flow.say: Before you turn the card over, tell me your exact words. Who would your action help? Could anyone get hurt?
flow.kid: Take a card. Choose an action. Say your exact words. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: Who does your action help, and could anyone get hurt by it?
good: It helps the child who is teased, and nobody is hurt.
If I pushed the bully, someone could get hurt, so I would tell a teacher.
It helps everyone who uses the place.

flow.parent: Some cards have two good choices. Accept either one. If your child chooses to fight or to shout, ask who might get hurt, and let them choose again.
flow.context: In this step of Kind and Safe you take situation cards, choose an action and check the back.

flow.do: Find the three cards whose backs begin ALWAYS TELL. Lay them side by side. Ask what they have in common.
flow.say: These three cards all say ALWAYS TELL. What is the same about them? Name two grown-ups you would tell.
flow.kid: Find the three ALWAYS TELL cards. What is the same about them? Name two grown-ups you trust.

check.q: Which situation should a child always tell a trusted grown-up about?
options: Someone is being hurt or threatened
check.why: When someone is being hurt, threatened or asked to keep a frightening secret, a child cannot fix it alone, so a grown-up must know. If you chose the wrapper, that is something you can put right yourself.

flow.parent: Make sure your child names at least two trusted grown-ups, and knows they can tell either one about anything that feels too big.
flow.context: This is the last step of Kind and Safe. You look at the situations that always need a trusted grown-up.

games.title: Keep the Lane Clean: a dice game about how litter spreads
games.context: This is a dice game that the players win or lose together. Each roll of the die is a passer-by, who drops a wrapper more often when the lane already has wrappers. The players have only five chances to pick one up.

printables.title: 6 boxes in a row: the lane
items: Lane box 6. If this box is filled, the lane is a dump

printables.title: 5 pick-up cards
items: PICK UP: take one wrapper out of the lane.
PICK UP: take one wrapper out of the lane.
PICK UP: take one wrapper out of the lane.
PICK UP: take one wrapper out of the lane.
PICK UP: take one wrapper out of the lane.

printables.title: Tally sheet, one for each round
items: Passers-by so far: make one mark for each roll, up to 20
Wrappers in the lane at the end

rules: You also need one die from any board game. Put 2 wrapper tokens in the lane, one to a box. Share out the 5 pick-up cards among the players.
Take turns. On your turn, roll the die for one passer-by, and make a mark on the tally sheet.
Count the wrappers in the lane. If the die shows that number or a smaller one, the passer-by drops a wrapper. Add one token.
A roll of 1 always adds a wrapper, even when the lane is empty. A few people drop litter anywhere.
After the roll, the player may use one pick-up card to take one wrapper out of the lane. A used card is out of the game.
If all 6 boxes are filled, the lane has become a dump, and all the players lose.
If 20 passers-by have gone by and a box is still empty, all the players win. The score is the number of wrappers left, and a lower score is better.
Then play a second round that starts with 4 wrappers in the lane. Compare the two rounds.
Playing alone? Hold all 5 pick-up cards yourself.

setup.art: A paper strip of six boxes on a table with two paper wrapper tokens in the first two boxes, a die, and five small cards marked PICK UP.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 wrappers in the lane. Share out the 5 pick-up cards.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the lane and making a tally mark on a sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Roll for each passer-by. If the die shows the number of wrappers or less, add a wrapper.

setup.art: A child laying down a PICK UP card and lifting one wrapper token out of the lane.
setup.caption: 3. After a roll, you may use a pick-up card to take one wrapper out.

flow.do: Cut out the lane, the tokens and the cards. Read the rules together. Ask the question below before the first roll.
flow.say: You have only five pick-up cards for twenty passers-by. Will you use them early or save them? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You have five pick-up cards. Will you use them early or late? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Lane Clean. You set up the lane and decide how to use your pick-up cards.

flow.do: Play the first round, starting with 2 wrappers. Stop at 20 passers-by or at a full lane. Write the score.
flow.say: Before each roll, tell me how many numbers on the die will add a wrapper now.
flow.kid: Roll for each passer-by. Say which numbers add a wrapper. Pick up when you choose.
flow.parent: With 2 wrappers, the numbers 1 and 2 add a wrapper. With 4 wrappers, the numbers 1 to 4 do. Players who pick up early nearly always win this round. Players who save their cards usually lose.
flow.context: In this step of Keep the Lane Clean you play a round that starts with 2 wrappers.

flow.do: Play the second round, starting with 4 wrappers and all 5 pick-up cards. Write the score.
flow.say: Now the lane starts with four wrappers. Do you expect this round to be easier or harder? Why?
flow.kid: Start with four wrappers. Is this round easier or harder? Why?
flow.parent: This round is lost about three times in four, even with careful play. Let your child feel the difference from the first round.
flow.context: In this step of Keep the Lane Clean you play a round that starts with 4 wrappers.

flow.do: Compare the two tally sheets. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at both rounds. When did one pick-up card help the most? What does that tell you about a real lane?
flow.kid: Compare the two rounds. When did a pick-up card help the most?

check.q: In Keep the Lane Clean, when does one pick-up card help the most?
options: Early, when few wrappers lie there
Late, when the lane is nearly full
check.why: With few wrappers, few passers-by copy, so one pick-up keeps the lane clean for many turns. If you chose 'late', look at the second round: with 4 wrappers, four numbers on the die add another.

flow.context: This is the last step of Keep the Lane Clean. You compare a lane that started with 2 wrappers and a lane that started with 4.

experiments.title: The Hurry Test: does another person's hurrying change where your chana land?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop 15 chana into a bottle, six times. Three runs are calm and three are hurried by a helper's words. You count the misses and your own pulse, to see what another person's words do to your body.
experiments.question: Do you miss the bottle more often when a helper hurries you than when the helper stays quiet? Does your pulse change too?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many of the 15 chana will miss in a calm run, and how many in a hurried run? Will your pulse change? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bottle, the same 15 chana and the same hand height every time. Sit in the same place. Take turns between calm and hurried runs, so that getting better with practice does not fool you. The helper says only one kind of thing: nothing, or hurry words. Only what the helper says changes.

materials.item: an empty 1-litre plastic water bottle with the cap off, and a 500 millilitre bottle as a spare
a steel plate or a tray with a rim, to stand the bottle on
dry chana, 15 pieces
a bowl for the chana
a ruler or a tape measure
a clock or phone with seconds, held by the helper
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: The helper uses only the words 'faster', 'hurry' and 'time is running out', in a playful voice. The helper never says anything unkind. Stop at once if the child is upset. Pick up every chana from the floor.

schedule.what: Practise, then do six runs that take turns between calm and hurried. Swap roles so that the grown-up is tested too.

experiments.record: Draw the table. Fill one row for each run. Under it, write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A 1-litre plastic bottle with its cap off stands on a steel plate, with a bowl of 15 chana beside it and a ruler held up to show 30 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the bottle on the plate. Hold each chana 30 cm above its mouth.

setup.art: A girl dropping one chana towards the bottle while a helper sits quietly beside her with a clock in her lap.
setup.caption: 2. In a calm run, the helper says 'Go' and then says nothing.

setup.art: The same girl dropping a chana while the helper leans forward and calls out 'Faster! Hurry!', with small lines showing the quick words.
setup.caption: 3. In a hurried run, the helper calls out 'Faster! Hurry!' all the way through.

setup.art: The girl holding two fingers on the inside of her wrist while the helper holds up a phone clock.
setup.caption: 4. After each run, count your pulse for 15 seconds. Then count the chana on the plate.

flow.do: Stand the bottle in the middle of the plate. Put 15 chana in the bowl. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will drop 15 chana into the bottle, one at a time. In some runs I stay quiet. In some runs I hurry you. How many will miss in each kind? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop 15 chana into the bottle. Will hurry words change your aim? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might hurry words change where a chana goes?
good: My hand might shake.
I might rush and aim badly.
My body might get tense or nervous.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The helper only says 'faster', 'hurry' and 'time is running out'. Never say 'you are slow'. Stop at once if your child is upset.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hurry Test. You set up the bottle and guess what another person's hurrying will do to your aim.

flow.do: Your child sits and holds each chana 30 cm above the bottle's mouth, about the length of a school ruler. They practise one round of 15 drops. The helper says nothing. Do not count this round.
flow.say: Hold each chana at the height of the ruler, then let go. Practise all 15 once. This round does not count.
flow.kid: Hold each chana 30 cm above the bottle. Drop all 15 for practice.
flow.parent: If every chana goes in, raise the hand to 45 cm, or use the 500 millilitre bottle, which has a smaller mouth. You want about 1 to 3 misses in a calm round. If chana keep missing, lower the hand to 20 cm.
flow.context: In this step of the Hurry Test you practise one round of 15 drops, so that the real runs are fair.

flow.do: Do the first pair of runs. Calm run: the helper says 'Go', then stays silent. Count the chana on the plate. Count the pulse for 15 seconds. Then do a hurried run: the helper says 'Go', then calls 'Faster! Hurry! Time is running out!' all the way through. Count both again.
flow.say: First a calm run. I say 'Go' and nothing more. Afterwards we count the chana on the plate, and your pulse for 15 seconds. Then the hurried run.
flow.kid: Do one calm run and one hurried run. Count misses. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.

check.q: In the Hurry Test, why do the calm and hurried runs take turns?
options: So practice does not fool us
So the chana do not break
check.why: If all the calm runs came first, you would get better by practice, and the hurried runs would look worse for that reason. Taking turns spreads the practice evenly. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test changes one thing only.

flow.parent: For the pulse, put two fingers on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb. Count the beats for 15 seconds. Write the misses, the pulse, and a body tightness number from 1 (loose) to 5 (very tight). Ask for the number straight after the run.
flow.context: In this step of the Hurry Test you do the first calm run and the first hurried run.

flow.do: Do four more runs in this order: calm, hurried, calm, hurried. Write down the misses, the pulse and the tightness number after every run. Rest for a minute if your child's arm is tired.
flow.say: Now four more runs, taking turns: calm, hurried, calm, hurried. Write down the three numbers after each one.
flow.kid: Do four more runs: calm, hurried, calm, hurried. Write three numbers each time.
flow.parent: A few families see no difference. That is a real result, and you can say so in the last step. Do not hint to your child what you hope to see.
flow.context: In this step of the Hurry Test you finish the six runs, taking turns between calm and hurried.

flow.do: Swap places. Your child is the helper. The grown-up does one calm run and one hurried run. The child counts the misses and the pulse. The grown-up says how tight their own body felt.
flow.say: Now you are the helper. I will do one calm run and one hurried run. Hurry me as I hurried you, and no more. Then count my misses and my pulse.
flow.kid: Now you are the helper. Hurry your grown-up in one run. Count their misses.
flow.parent: Let your child hear how the hurry words feel from the helper's side. Ask them afterwards how it felt to hurry someone.
flow.context: In this step of the Hurry Test the grown-up takes the test, and the child is the helper.

flow.do: Add up the misses of the three calm runs and of the three hurried runs. Compare the pulses and the tightness numbers. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Add up the misses in the three calm runs, and in the three hurried runs. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Add up the misses for each kind of run. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Did the hurried runs have more misses than the calm runs? What else changed?
good: Yes, there were more misses, and my pulse was higher.
My body felt tighter.
Not much changed, and that is a real result too.

ask.q: How could you find out whether the words or only the speed caused the misses?
good: Hurry myself with no words, then compare.
Have the helper say 'faster' in a slow, calm voice.
Run the same test with a helper who says 'take your time'.

flow.parent: The reason: hurry words can set off the stress response. Adrenaline speeds the heart, and the muscles tighten. Tight, quick hands aim less well. The test cannot separate the words from the speed, and a grown-up can say so honestly. A small test of one family is only a hint. Scientists would repeat it with many people.
flow.think: Think of a time someone hurried you. What did your body do?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hurry Test. You add up your six runs and say what another person's words did to your hand.

experiments.title: The Smile Count: does a smile come back more often than a plain face?
experiments.context: In this experiment you greet 10 people with a smile and a word, and 10 people with a plain face and no word. You count how many smile back. It tests whether a face spreads from one person to another.
experiments.question: Out of 10 people, how many smile back at a smile and a greeting, and how many smile back at a plain face?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many of 10 people will smile back at a smile? How many at a plain face? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Greet people one after another, taking turns: smile, plain, smile, plain. Use the same places and the same time of day. A plain face is a calm, ordinary face, never a cross one. Only the smile and the word change. Count a smile back only if it comes within 3 seconds.

materials.item: a grown-up who walks with the child the whole time
a notebook page and a pencil, for tally marks
a place where many people pass, such as the building's stairs, the gate, the lane or a shop queue

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child all the time. Greet only people who pass you in public places. Never stop anyone, follow anyone or ask anyone a question. If someone seems upset, do not greet them.

schedule.what: Walk to a place where people pass. Greet 10 people with a smile and 10 with a plain face, taking turns. The grown-up keeps the tally.

experiments.record: Make a table with two rows: smile and word, plain face. Write the number of people, the number who smiled back and the number who said something back.

setup.art: A girl and her mother standing near the gate of a block of flats, with a notebook page of tally marks in the mother's hand.
setup.caption: 1. Go with a grown-up to a place where people pass. The grown-up keeps the tally.

setup.art: The girl smiling and nodding at a passing neighbour, who smiles back.
setup.caption: 2. To one person, give a smile and a greeting.

setup.art: The girl with a calm plain face looking at the next passer-by, who walks on.
setup.caption: 3. To the next person, give a plain face and no word. Take turns.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns of tally marks, one headed Smile and one headed Plain.
setup.caption: 4. After 10 of each, add up the tally marks.

flow.do: Read the plan together. Choose the place. Ask your child for the guess and the reason, and write both down. Practise a plain face in a mirror, calm and not cross.
flow.say: You will greet 10 people with a smile and a word, and 10 with a plain face. How many will smile back each way? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will smile at some people and not at others. Guess who smiles back more. Why?

ask.q: Why might someone smile back at a stranger's smile?
good: Smiling is catching.
It is polite.
Seeing a smile makes my own face copy it.

flow.parent: Choose a place where about 20 people pass in 15 to 20 minutes. A big building's stairs, a lane near a shop or a bus stop will do. If few people pass, do it over two days. The plain face is a calm resting face, not a frown.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Smile Count. You guess how many people will smile back at a smile, and at a plain face.

flow.do: Stand with your child at the place. Your child greets passers-by, taking turns: smile and a word, then a plain face and no word, until 10 of each. Use a tally mark for each person. Mark a smile back only if it comes within 3 seconds.
flow.say: Greet the first person with a smile and a word. The next person gets a plain face. I will make a tally mark for each person who smiles back.
flow.kid: Greet people in turns: smile and a word, then a plain face. Your grown-up keeps the tally.

check.q: In the Smile Count, why must the plain face be calm and not cross?
options: So only the smile is different
check.why: A cross face could also change what people do. Then we would not know if the smile or the cross face made the difference. If you chose another answer, remember to change one thing only.

flow.parent: Use the local greeting, such as 'good morning', 'vanakkam', 'namaste' or 'salaam'. Say it in an ordinary voice. Some people look at phones and do not see the child. Count them as people greeted only if they looked at the child.
flow.context: In this step of the Smile Count you greet 10 people with a smile and a word, and 10 with a plain face.

flow.do: Add up the tally marks for each way of greeting. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Add up the smiles that came back each way. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Add up the smiles that came back. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Did more people smile back at a smile than at a plain face?
good: Yes, about twice as many.
The numbers were about the same.
A few people smiled at both.

ask.q: How could someone smile back without wanting to?
good: Our face muscles copy a face we see.
The copying can happen very fast.

flow.parent: The reason: when we see a face, our own face muscles begin to copy it, often within half a second, and the copied look can start the feeling. So smiles are catching. A smile that comes back is a hint, not proof, because some people smile to be polite. If the numbers are about equal, say so: a big city, a hurry or a phone can stop people looking up.
flow.think: If one smile can start another, what might a frown start?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Smile Count. You compare the smiles that came back after a smile and after a plain face.

experiments.title: The Doorway Test: which doors and switches in your home fit a wheelchair?
experiments.context: In this experiment you measure the doors, thresholds and switches in your home. You compare them with the size of a wheelchair and the reach of a seated person. It shows which parts of a place stop some people from using it.
experiments.question: How many of the doors, thresholds and switches in your home can a person in a wheelchair use?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many of the five doors in your home will let a 65 cm wide wheelchair pass? Which will not? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure the narrowest point of each door with the door fully open. Measure from the floor, always the same way. Use the same tape or ruler every time. Measure in centimetres and write the number down before you decide if it passes.

materials.item: a tape measure, or a long string and a ruler
a piece of string 65 cm long, with a knot at each end
a piece of string 90 cm long, with a knot at each end
masking tape or a few sticky notes
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do not climb on anything to reach a switch. Measure only. Do not switch on any heavy appliance or touch any open wire.

schedule.what: Measure five doors, any threshold or step, and the heights of switches, taps and handles. Compare them with a wheelchair and a seated person.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each door, step, switch and handle. Write the measurement and tick yes or no. At the bottom, write the one change that would help the most.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: No, a 65 cm wheelchair is wider
Narrow, a 65 cm wheelchair just passes

setup.art: A girl holding a 65 centimetre knotted string across the open bathroom door of a flat, with a tape measure in her other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the 65 cm string across each open door. Measure the narrowest gap.

setup.art: A girl crouching to measure the height of a step at a bathroom door with a ruler standing on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Measure any step or edge on the floor at a doorway.

setup.art: A girl standing at a wall with two pieces of masking tape marking 40 cm and 120 cm up from the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Mark 40 cm and 120 cm on a wall. A seated person reaches between these marks.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of doors and switches and a yes or no beside each.
setup.caption: 4. Write each measurement. Tick yes or no.

flow.do: Cut two pieces of string, 65 cm and 90 cm, and tie a knot at each end. Tell your child that an ordinary wheelchair is about 65 cm wide. Guides ask for a clear door width of at least 90 cm. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: A common wheelchair is about 65 centimetres wide. Which of our doors do you think it can pass? Which will it not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A wheelchair is about 65 cm wide. Which doors at home will it pass? Why?

ask.q: Why might a bathroom door be narrower than a front door?
good: A bathroom is small, and people planned it for walking.
The builder saved space.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Cut the strings carefully. Mark the 65 cm one with a knot at each end. Wheelchair widths vary from about 60 to 70 cm, so 65 cm is a fair middle size.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Doorway Test. You make two measuring strings and guess which doors in your home a wheelchair can pass.

flow.do: Open each of five doors fully, such as the front door, the bathroom, the kitchen, a bedroom and the balcony. Hold the 65 cm string across the narrowest gap. Then measure the gap with the tape. Write the number.
flow.say: Open the door fully. Does the 65 centimetre string fit across the narrowest gap? Measure it and write the number.
flow.kid: Open each door fully. Measure the narrowest gap. Does the 65 cm string fit?

check.q: In the Doorway Test, which part of a door do you measure?
options: The narrowest gap with the door open
The width of the door itself
check.why: A wheelchair must pass the narrowest point. The open door and its handle often take up some of the width. If you chose the width of the door, remember that the door itself can stand in the way.

flow.parent: The clear width is smaller than the door leaf, because the open door and its handle stand in the way. Measure the gap between the frame and the open door. Narrow doors are common in older bathrooms.
flow.context: In this step of the Doorway Test you measure five doors in your home.

flow.do: At each doorway, look for a step or a raised edge on the floor. Stand a ruler upright on the floor and measure its height. Write the number. A small front wheel can be stopped by a low raised edge.
flow.say: Look at the floor at each doorway. Is there a step or a raised edge? Stand the ruler up beside it and measure the height.
flow.kid: Look for steps at each doorway. Measure their height.
flow.parent: Many bathrooms have a raised edge to hold water in. A grown-up, a trolley or a pram can bump over it. A wheelchair often cannot.
flow.context: In this step of the Doorway Test you measure the steps and raised edges at the doorways.

flow.do: Mark 40 cm and 120 cm up a wall with masking tape. Guides say controls should sit between these marks for a seated person to reach. Measure three switches, the door handle and a tap from the floor. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Stick tape at 40 and 120 centimetres up the wall. A seated person reaches between the tapes. Measure the switches, a handle and a tap from the floor.
flow.kid: Put tape at 40 and 120 cm on the wall. Measure a switch, a handle and a tap.
flow.parent: A grown-up holds the ruler for anything above your child's reach. Many fan and light switches sit high on the wall, at the top of that range or above it. The aim is only to measure, so no one climbs.
flow.think: Who else, apart from a person in a wheelchair, finds a high switch hard to reach?
flow.context: In this step of the Doorway Test you measure how high the switches, handles and taps in your home are.

flow.do: Look at the table. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then ask for one change that would help the most, and whether it would also help others.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Which one change would help the most?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Is the narrow door the person's problem, or the building's?
good: The building's, because it was made for people who walk.
A person cannot change a door by trying harder.

ask.q: Who else would a wider door, a lower switch or a ramp help?
good: A grandparent with a walking frame.
A parent with a pram.
Someone carrying shopping.

flow.parent: The reason: a barrier is anything in a place that stops some people from using it. It is not the person who is the problem, it is the way the place was built. Changes made for one person often help many. If you find barriers, that is nothing to feel bad about. Nearly every home has them. A wedge, a mat or a moved plant can fix small ones.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Doorway Test. You say which parts of your home stop some people, and what one change would help.

activities.title: Three Good Places: why do you like them?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You name three places where you feel happy and safe. Then you sort your reasons into the people in them and the things in them.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
two coloured pens

activities.record: Write the three places. Under each, write two reasons. Mark each reason P for people and how they act, or T for things in the place.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three place names written across the top and two reasons written under each.
setup.caption: 1. Write three places where you feel happy and safe. Give two reasons for each.

setup.art: The same sheet with each reason marked P or T in two colours.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each reason P for people and how they act, or T for things in the place.

flow.do: Ask your child to name three places where they feel happy and safe. They give two reasons for each, and you write them down. Ask the guess below before the sorting.
flow.say: Name three places where you feel happy and safe. Give me two reasons for each. Then guess: will most reasons be about the people there, or about the things there? Why?
flow.kid: Name three places where you feel happy and safe. Give two reasons for each.
flow.parent: Accept every place, such as a grandmother's house, a temple steps, a bedroom corner or a school. Do not correct the reasons.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Good Places. You name places where you feel happy and safe, and say why.

flow.do: Mark each reason P if it is about people and how they act, such as 'nobody shouts'. Mark it T if it is about things, such as 'it has a swing'. Count the P marks and the T marks.
flow.say: Mark each reason. Use P if it is about people and how they act. Use T if it is about things in the place. Then count each letter.
flow.kid: Mark each reason P for people or T for things. Count each letter.

ask.q: Which letter did you write more often?
good: P, most of my reasons are about people.
T, most of my reasons are about things.
They were about equal.

flow.parent: Many children write more P marks, but not all do. Both are fine. Note that 'it is clean' looks like a T but is partly about people too, because people keep it clean.
flow.context: In this step of Three Good Places you sort your reasons into people and things.

flow.do: Ask the questions below. Listen to the answers. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Think of a beautiful new building where people shout at each other. Would you be happy there? Now think of a plain room where everyone is kind. Which would you pick? Why?
flow.kid: Think of two places. One is new, but the people are unkind. The other is plain, but the people are kind. Which do you pick?

check.q: Which part of a place most decides whether it is a happy one?
options: How the people in it treat each other
check.why: A plain place with kind people is usually a happier place than a fine place with unkind people. If you chose the building, think about the places on your list again.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Good Places. You think about whether the people or the building matter more.

activities.title: The E on Your Forehead: whose point of view do you take?
activities.context: This is a quick activity about seeing a place, or a letter, from another person's side. You draw a capital E on your own forehead with a finger. Then you check which way round you drew it.

materials.item: two or more people sitting facing each other
a finger each

activities.record: Write how many people drew the E so that they could read it, and how many drew it so that the watcher could read it.

setup.art: A girl facing her father across a table, drawing a capital E on her own forehead with one finger.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a capital E on your own forehead, quickly, with one finger.

setup.art: The father looking at the girl's forehead and nodding at the direction of the three short lines of the E.
setup.caption: 2. The watcher sees which way the three short lines point.

flow.do: Sit facing your child. Say: 'Draw a big capital E on your own forehead with one finger. Do it quickly, without stopping to plan.' Watch the three short lines of the E. Write which way they pointed. Then swap roles.
flow.say: Draw a big capital E on your own forehead with one finger. Do it quickly, without stopping to plan.
flow.kid: Draw a capital E on your forehead with one finger. Be quick.
flow.parent: If the three short lines point to the drawer's right ear, the drawer can read the E, and the watcher sees it backwards. If they point to the drawer's left ear, the watcher can read it. Write down who drew which. Do not say what it means yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the E on Your Forehead. You draw an E on your own forehead, and a watcher looks at it.

flow.do: Ask each person how they drew it, and which way the short lines pointed. Then try again. This time say: 'Draw the E so that I can read it.' Check what each person did.
flow.say: Which way did you draw your E? Who could read it, you or the watcher? Now draw it again so that the watcher can read it. Is it harder?
flow.kid: Which way did you draw it? Now draw it so the watcher can read it.

ask.q: When you drew it quickly, who could read it, you or the watcher?
good: I could. The watcher saw it backwards.
The watcher could.
I did not think about it.

flow.parent: Many people draw it so that they can read it, and many draw it so that others can. Neither is wrong. Researchers have found that people who are thinking about themselves are more likely to draw it for themselves. This is a small game and not a test of a person's kindness.
flow.context: In this step of the E on Your Forehead you check which way you drew it, and then you draw it for the watcher.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Then say that places are built the same way, by people who think about their own view.
flow.say: Why might a person draw the E for themselves? A place can be built from one person's side, too. Where have you seen that?
flow.kid: A place can be built from one person's side. Where have you seen that?

ask.q: Where have you seen a place built from only one person's side?
good: A switch that is too high for a child to reach.
A step with no ramp.
A notice written in only one language.

flow.context: This is the last step of the E on Your Forehead. You connect it to places that are built from one person's point of view.
