activities.title: Lost for Words: what helps when you do not know the language?
activities.context: In this activity you give an instruction in a language the other person does not know. You try saying it again, then louder, then pointing, then showing. You count which way works. It helps you welcome a child new to your language.

materials.item: a steel cup
a spoon
a plate
a language one of you knows and the other does not, or made-up sounds

activities.record: Draw a table with four rows: said again, said louder, pointed, showed. Write a tick if the helper understood the instruction.

setup.art: A mother saying a sentence to her daughter, who holds up empty palms, with a cup, a spoon and a plate on the table between them.
setup.caption: 1. Give an instruction in a language the other person does not know.

setup.art: The mother pointing at the spoon and then at the cup, with the daughter beginning to smile.
setup.caption: 2. Try louder, then pointing, then showing. Tick the ways that work.

flow.do: Put a cup, a spoon and a plate on the table. Choose a language that your child does not know. Use a language that someone in the family speaks, or use made-up sounds. Say an instruction, such as 'put the spoon in the cup', in that language. Ask your child what they think will help.
flow.say: I will give you an instruction in a language you do not know. What do you think will help you to understand? Why?
flow.kid: I will speak to you in a language you do not know. What will help? Why?
flow.parent: If no one in the family knows a language your child does not know, use made-up sounds with a question tune. Say them in an ordinary voice, as if they were real words. Do not use a mocking voice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lost for Words. You guess what helps when you are given an instruction in a language you do not know.

flow.do: Give the same instruction four ways. First say it once, in an ordinary voice. Then say it louder. Then point at the spoon and the cup as you say it. Last, do it yourself while your child watches. Tick each way that works.
flow.say: I will give the same instruction four ways. Say it once. Say it louder. Say it and point. Do it while they watch. Tick the ones that work.
flow.kid: Try four ways: say it, say it louder, point, show. Tick each one that works.

ask.q: Which way worked first? Did the louder way help?
good: Louder did not help.
Pointing helped.
Showing worked every time.

check.q: In Lost for Words, why does saying it louder not help?
options: The words are the same, and still not understood
Loud voices are hard to hear
check.why: The loudness is not the problem. The listener does not know the words. Pointing and showing add something the listener can understand. If you chose another answer, think about what changed in each try.

flow.parent: The result is almost always the same. Louder does not help. Pointing helps a little. Showing works best. Swap roles after the first round, so your child gives an instruction in made-up sounds to you. Many children enjoy this.
flow.context: In this step of Lost for Words you give the same instruction four ways and tick the ways that work.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Write down a plan for welcoming a new child who does not know your language.
flow.say: A new child joins your class. She does not know your language. What are three things you could do to help her?
flow.kid: A new child does not know your language. What can you do to help?

ask.q: What could you do to help a new child who does not know your language?
good: Point and show what to do.
Sit with her at lunch.
Learn one word of her language.
Use pictures.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lost for Words. You make a plan to welcome a child who does not know your language.

activities.title: What Helped? Which calming move slows your pulse best?
activities.context: In the Hurry Test you counted your pulse after hurried runs. In this activity you raise your pulse by marching for a minute. Then you try three ways to settle, and keep a log of what helped. It shows how a big feeling in the body can settle.

materials.item: a clock or phone that shows seconds
a notebook page and a pencil
a chair

activities.safety: March on the spot at an easy pace, not a run. Stop at once if you feel dizzy or unwell. A grown-up stays with the child.
activities.record: Draw the What Helped? log with a row for each move: pulse at the start, pulse at the end, and the feeling size at the start and end, from 1 (small) to 5 (big).

setup.art: A girl marching on the spot with a clock on a chair beside her and a grown-up counting seconds.
setup.caption: 1. March on the spot for 1 minute, at an easy pace.

setup.art: The girl sitting on the chair counting her pulse for 15 seconds with two fingers on her wrist.
setup.caption: 2. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The girl sitting with her hand on her tummy, breathing in for three counts and out for six counts.
setup.caption: 3. Settle in one of three ways, for 1 minute. Count your pulse again.

flow.do: Show your child how to count the pulse: two fingers on the inside of the wrist, for 15 seconds. Show the slow out-breath: breathe in for 3 counts, out for 6. Ask the guess below.
flow.say: We will try three ways to settle your body. One is to sit still. One is to breathe out slowly. One is to say how you feel and tell me. Which will slow your pulse most? Why?
flow.kid: Try three ways to settle. Which will slow your pulse most? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any answer with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of What Helped? You learn to count your pulse and breathe out slowly, and you guess which move will help most.

flow.do: Do three trials, with a 3-minute rest between them. In each trial: March on the spot for 1 minute. Count the pulse for 15 seconds, and write it. Give the feeling a size from 1 to 5. Then settle for 1 minute in one of three ways. Trial A: sit still. Trial B: sit and breathe in for 3 counts and out for 6. Trial C: say aloud 'I feel puffed and a bit silly', and tell the grown-up about your day. Count the pulse again and write the feeling size.
flow.say: March for one minute. Count your pulse. Give your feeling a size from one to five. Then settle for one minute in one of three ways. Count the pulse again.
flow.kid: March one minute. Count your pulse. Settle one minute. Count again.
flow.parent: A few beats of difference are normal from one trial to the next. One trial is not enough to decide. If you want a fairer test, repeat the next day in the order C, B, A. The body is revved by marching, not by a feeling, but a strong feeling revs the body in a similar way.
flow.context: In this step of What Helped? you try three ways to settle your body and write down what happens.

flow.do: Look at the log together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Ask for the move they will try the next time they feel a big feeling.
flow.say: Look at your log. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Which move would you try next time you feel a big feeling?
flow.kid: Look at your log. Which move helped most? Which will you try next time?

ask.q: Which move slowed your pulse the most? Did it also make you feel better?
good: Breathing out slowly.
Sitting still.
Saying how I felt.
They were about the same.

check.q: In What Helped?, why is one trial not enough to decide?
options: Pulse varies a little each time by chance
check.why: A pulse changes a few beats from one try to the next, even with the same move. So one number tells us little. If you chose another answer, think about repeating the trial.

flow.parent: What science says: the body clears adrenaline within minutes, if nothing sets off more. A long out-breath slows the heart a little. Naming a feeling, moving and talking to a person you trust also help. What helps most differs from person to person. If a feeling is too big or does not go away, tell a trusted grown-up. Do not diagnose or label your child.
flow.think: Which of the three moves could you do in a classroom without anyone noticing?
flow.context: This is the last step of What Helped? You say which way of settling helped your body most.

activities.title: Know Their Name: ask one worker about their day
activities.context: This is an activity about the people who keep a building running. You greet one of them by name and ask four polite questions about their day. Then you write the day as they might live it.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a grown-up to stand beside the child

activities.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child all the time. Ask permission first. Never ask about money, caste, religion or private matters. If the person says no, thank them and stop.
activities.record: Write the person's name and job. Write what they told you in four lines. Then write 8 lines of how their day might feel to them. Mark which are what they said and which you imagine.

setup.art: A girl and her father greeting a woman who sweeps the lane beside a block of flats, with the girl smiling and asking a question.
setup.caption: 1. Greet a worker by name. Ask if you may ask four questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with four short lines of answers and then eight lines of the day written below.
setup.caption: 2. Write what they told you. Then write how their day might feel to them.

flow.do: Choose a person who works near your building, such as the watchman, the cleaner or the milk seller. Find out their name. Ask if they have two minutes. Ask your child for the guess below first.
flow.say: We will meet one person who works near our home. What do you think is the hardest part of their day? What is the best part? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will meet a person who works near us. Guess the hardest part of their day. Why?
flow.parent: Choose a person who knows you a little, so that your child is not a stranger. Ask first, so that they can say no. A greeting by name is already respect.
flow.context: This is the first step of Know Their Name. You choose a person who works near your home and guess what their day is like.

flow.do: Your child greets the person by name and asks four questions. First, what time does the day start? Second, what is done first? Third, what is the hardest part? Last, what would make it easier? Your child writes the answers in short lines.
flow.say: Greet them by name and ask if you may ask four questions. What time does your day start? What do you do first? What is hardest? What would make it easier?
flow.kid: Greet them by name. Ask four questions. Write the answers.

check.q: Which question is not right to ask a person who has just agreed to talk?
options: How much money do you earn?
What time does your day start?
What would make your day easier?
check.why: A person's pay is private, and asking can embarrass them. The other two ask about their work and what would help. If you chose another one, think about which questions the person could answer comfortably.

flow.parent: Let the person say as much or as little as they like. Say thank you, and use their name. If they say what would make the day easier, listen and do not promise anything you cannot do.
flow.context: In this step of Know Their Name you ask one worker four polite questions about their day.

flow.do: At home, your child writes 8 lines about the person's day, as the person. They start from what the person said. They mark what was said and what was imagined. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Write eight lines about their day, as if you were them. Mark what they told you, and what you imagined. What could our building change to make it easier?
flow.kid: Write eight lines about their day, as them. Mark what they said and what you imagined.

ask.q: What could our building change to make this person's day easier?
good: Keep the lane free of rubbish.
Wrap broken glass.
Greet them every day.
Keep wet and dry waste apart.

flow.parent: Point of view means working out what someone sees, knows and needs from where they are. It is a guess, and the person's own words are the best evidence. Notice any step in the person's day where our own habits make it harder, such as mixed waste or a blocked lane.
flow.context: This is the last step of Know Their Name. You write the person's day from their point of view.

projects.title: Our Charter: five rules for a place we share, and a week to try them
projects.context: In this four-day project your family writes five rules for a place you share, signs them, and ticks each day which rules were kept. It tests whether rules that people agree on together last longer.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or chart paper
a pencil and a pen for each person
tape or a pin to put the charter on a wall
a grown-up to help the family meeting

projects.safety: Keep it friendly. A rule is for everyone, including the grown-ups. Nobody is blamed.

schedule.what: Choose a place you share. Look at it for 5 minutes. List three things that go wrong there.
Hold a family meeting. Each person says one rule. Choose five, write them, and everyone signs.
Tick each rule kept or not kept. Notice who did it first.
Tick again. Count the ticks. Change one rule if it does not work, and say why.

projects.record: Write the five rules and the signatures. Draw a grid with the five rules down the side and the days across. Tick each rule kept. At the end, write which rule was kept most and why.

setup.art: A family sitting round a table in a flat, each person saying one rule while one child writes on a large sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a family meeting. Each person says one rule.

setup.art: A large sheet titled Our Charter with five short rules and four signatures, pinned to the wall beside the shoe rack.
setup.caption: 2. Write five rules and let everyone sign. Pin the sheet where all can see it.

setup.art: A tick grid on the same sheet with five rules down the side and four days across.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, tick the rules that were kept.

flow.do: Day 1. Choose a place the whole family uses, such as the entrance, the study corner or the kitchen. Look at it for 5 minutes. Write three things that often go wrong there. Ask for the guess below.
flow.say: Pick a place we all share. Look at it carefully. What goes wrong there? Which of the three things do you think will be hardest to fix? Why?
flow.kid: Pick a place we all share. List three things that go wrong. Guess the hardest to fix.
flow.parent: Shoes at the door, a tap left running, noise during study time and things not put back are common. Do not blame. Ask what the place looks like to a visitor.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Our Charter. You choose a place you share, and list three things that often go wrong there.

flow.do: Day 2. Hold a family meeting. Everyone says one rule that would help. Write 'We' rules that say what to do, such as 'We put shoes on the rack'. Choose five rules. Everyone signs. Pin the sheet on a wall.
flow.say: Each of us says one rule that would help the place. Write it as what we will do, not what we will not do. Then we choose five and everyone signs.
flow.kid: Each person says one rule. Write 'We' rules. Choose five. Everyone signs.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you choose the place

ask.q: Why does a rule written as 'We do' feel different from 'Do not'?
good: It says what to do, not just what is wrong.
It includes everyone.

flow.parent: Rules last longest when the people who use the place agree on them together. Take the grown-ups' rules seriously too. A signature means a person agrees, not that a person was told.
flow.context: In this step of Our Charter you hold a family meeting, write five rules and sign them.

flow.do: Day 3. Look at the charter. Tick each rule that was kept yesterday and today. Ask who did a rule first, without being asked.
flow.say: Which rules did we keep? Who started one without being asked? What did the others do when they saw that?
flow.kid: Tick each rule that was kept. Who started one first?
flow.wait: Do this the day after the charter is signed
flow.parent: Notice that rules are kept most when a person is seen doing them. Younger children copy older ones.
flow.context: In this step of Our Charter you tick which rules were kept, and notice who started them.

flow.do: Day 4. Tick again. Count the ticks for each rule. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Change one rule if it did not work.
flow.say: Count the ticks for each rule. Which rule was kept most? Which least? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Count the ticks. Which rule was kept most? Why?
flow.wait: Do this the day after day 3

ask.q: Which rule was kept most, and why do you think so?
good: The easy rules, such as putting shoes on the rack.
The one where a person did it first.
The one with a reminder right beside it.

flow.parent: A rule that is easy to do and easy to see tends to last. If a rule slipped, ask what would make it easier, such as a hook, a basket or a sign beside the place. Change one rule, with everyone's agreement, and sign again.
flow.context: This is the last day of Our Charter. You count which rules were kept and change one if it did not work.

challenges.title: The Ramp That Fits: a 15 cm step and only 120 cm of ground in front
challenges.context: In the Doorway Test you found that a step or a raised edge can stop a wheelchair. In this design challenge you plan a ramp for a 15 cm step at a library door. A scale model, with 1 cm standing for 10 cm, lets you test your plan.
challenges.problem: A library door has one step that is 15 cm high. Guides say a ramp may rise no more than 1 cm for every 12 cm of length. But the ground in front of the step is only 120 cm deep, because a wall stands there. The step itself is 600 cm wide. Design a ramp that a wheelchair can use.
constraints: In your model, 1 cm stands for 10 cm. The step is 1.5 cm high and 60 cm wide. The ground in front is 12 cm deep.
The ramp must rise 1.5 cm in total. It needs at least 12 cm of length for each 1 cm of rise. So the whole ramp needs at least 18 cm in your model.
The ramp must be at least 12 cm wide in the model, which stands for 120 cm.
Any turn needs a flat landing at least 15 cm long and 15 cm wide.
materials: thick card, a flat tray lid or a thin wooden board, cut into strips 12 cm wide
a notebook about 1.5 cm thick for the step
general: A straight ramp that runs sideways along the front of the step. It is 18 cm long and 12 cm deep.
A straight ramp that starts at one end of the step and rises as it runs along the wall.
A longer ramp that starts further along the step, so that the slope is gentler.
creative: A ramp that starts at one end of the step, turns on a landing, and ends at the door.
A ramp that curves along the front of the step in a gentle arc.
A ramp built from the side, where there is more ground, and joined to the path.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own ramp. Draw it from above and from the side. Write its total length, its rise and how many centimetres of length it has for each 1 cm of rise. Say who else it helps.

setup.art: A notebook 1.5 centimetres thick standing on a table with a ruler beside it, and a card wall behind it marking 12 centimetres of ground in front.
setup.caption: 1. Make the step from a notebook 1.5 cm thick. Mark 12 cm of ground in front of it.

setup.art: A strip of card lying straight out from the notebook to the floor with a toy car at the bottom and a ruler showing 12 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a 12 cm strip straight out from the step. Measure the rise and the length.

setup.art: An 18 centimetre strip of card lying sideways along the front of the notebook from the floor up to its top edge.
setup.caption: 3. Lay an 18 cm strip sideways along the front of the step instead.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Set up the model: a notebook 1.5 cm thick for the step, with a wall 12 cm in front of it. Ask your child for three ideas, and which they expect to work best.
flow.say: A library step is 15 centimetres high, and there are only 120 centimetres of ground in front. How could a wheelchair get up it? Which idea do you think will work best? Why?
flow.kid: A step is 15 cm high. The ground in front is only 120 cm. How could a wheelchair get up?

ask.q: Why can a ramp not be as short as the step is high?
good: It would be a very steep slope.
A wheelchair could tip back.
It would be hard to push.

flow.parent: In the model the step is 1.5 cm high. A straight ramp of 12 cm out from the step rises 1.5 cm in 12 cm, which is 1 cm of rise for 8 cm of length. That is steeper than the guide allows.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Ramp That Fits. You set up the model step and think of ways to get a wheelchair up it.

flow.do: Your child lays a card strip 12 cm long straight out from the step to the floor. They measure the rise and the length. They work out how many centimetres of length there are for each 1 cm of rise. They roll the toy car down it.
flow.say: Lay a strip of card 12 centimetres long, straight out from the step. How many centimetres of length do you have for each centimetre of rise?
flow.kid: Lay a 12 cm strip straight out from the step. How long is it for each 1 cm of rise?

check.q: A 12 cm ramp rises 1.5 cm. How many cm of length for each 1 cm of rise?
check.why: 12 divided by 1.5 is 8. The guide asks for at least 12 for each 1 cm of rise, so this ramp is too steep. If you chose 12, divide the length by the rise to check.

flow.parent: 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8. The guide asks for 12 or more. A toy car rolled down this ramp picks up speed quickly. Let your child feel that this ramp is too steep.
flow.context: In this step of The Ramp That Fits you test the ramp that fits straight out from the step, and work out its slope.

flow.do: Your child makes a ramp at least 18 cm long that still fits in the 12 cm of ground. They build it from card strips and tape. They measure its length and roll the toy car along it.
flow.say: Now make a ramp at least 18 centimetres long that still fits in 12 centimetres of ground. Remember that the step is 60 centimetres wide.
flow.kid: Make an 18 cm ramp that fits in 12 cm of ground.
flow.parent: The usual answer runs sideways along the front of the step. A strip 18 cm long and 12 cm wide fits in the 12 cm of ground. 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12, which just meets the guide. Accept any design that measures well.
flow.context: In this step of The Ramp That Fits you build a ramp that is long enough and still fits the space.

flow.do: Compare the two ramps. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Compare the two ramps. Which one would you rather push a wheelchair up? What does the longer ramp cost, and who does it help?
flow.kid: Compare the two ramps. Which is better? What does the longer ramp cost?

ask.q: Who else, apart from a person in a wheelchair, would a ramp help?
good: A parent with a pram.
A grandparent with a stick.
A worker with a trolley.
A child on a bicycle.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Ramp That Fits. You compare the short ramp and the long ramp.

challenges.title: A Notice Without Words: make a sign that anyone can follow
challenges.context: In Lost for Words, saying an instruction louder did not help, and pointing and showing did. Here you design a notice that needs no words. You test it on three people who have not seen it.
challenges.problem: A school has hooks for bags outside every classroom. Children keep dropping their bags on the floor, and new children who do not read the school's language do not know what to do. Design a notice with no words that shows children to hang their bags on the hooks.
constraints: The notice may use no words and no letters.
It may use at most three colours.
It must be understood from 2 metres away.
It works if at least 2 of 3 people who have not seen it say that it means: hang the bag on the hook.
materials: a sheet of white paper and a pencil
three people who have not seen your notice
general: A picture of a bag hanging on a hook, with a tick.
A picture of a bag on the floor with a cross.
An arrow pointing from a bag to the hook.
creative: Footprints on the floor that lead to the hook.
A hook painted in a bright colour on a plain wall.
A row of hooks each with a different picture, so that every child has their own.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own notice. Test it on three people. Write how many said the right thing. Say what you would change, and why.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a drawn bag, an arrow and a hook, with no words on it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a notice that uses no words.

setup.art: A girl holding up her notice to a neighbour, who is pointing at the hook in the drawing.
setup.caption: 2. Show it to a person who has not seen it. Ask what it means. Do not help.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Recall Lost for Words, where pointing and showing worked best. Ask your child for the guess below, and write it down.
flow.say: In Lost for Words, saying it louder did not help, and showing worked. What kind of picture will show 'hang your bag on the hook'? Which idea will work best? Why?
flow.kid: Showing worked in Lost for Words. What picture shows 'hang your bag'? Why?

ask.q: What helped most in Lost for Words?
good: Pointing.
Showing it.
Not saying it louder.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Notice Without Words. You recall what helped in Lost for Words and plan a notice.

flow.do: Your child draws a notice with no words and at most three colours.
flow.say: Draw your notice. Use no words and at most three colours. Make it big and clear.
flow.kid: Draw a notice with no words. Use at most three colours.
flow.parent: Let your child choose. Pictures with arrows, a tick and a cross work well. If they use a word by habit, rub it out and draw it instead.
flow.context: In this step of A Notice Without Words you draw a notice that uses no words.

flow.do: Show the notice to three people who have not seen it, from 2 metres away. Ask each: 'What does this tell you to do?' Do not help. Count how many say the right thing.
flow.say: Show your notice to three people. Ask each one what it tells them to do. Do not help. Count how many say hang the bag on the hook.
flow.kid: Show your notice to three people. Ask what it means. Count the right answers.

check.q: A notice works if how many of three people understand it?
check.why: Two of three means most people understand it. One of three is too few, and a rule of all three every time is hard to meet. If it fails, change it and test it again with new people.

ask.q: If a person got it wrong, what did your notice leave out?
good: The hook was not clear.
The arrow pointed the wrong way.
There were too many colours.

flow.parent: Use new people for each test, so no one has seen it before. If fewer than 2 get it, change one thing and test with three new people. This is how signs on roads are made.
flow.context: In this step of A Notice Without Words you test your notice on three people.

worksheets.title: Happy places, feelings that spread, and kind and safe actions

items.p: Which three things make a place a happy one?
opts: Safety, belonging and care for the place
New paint, big rooms and loud music
items.why: A happy place is one where people are safe, everyone belongs, and the place is cared for. Paint, size and prizes can help, but they do not make a place happy on their own.

items.p: Match each action to what it does.
pairs: Uses a steady voice and few words
Sits or stands with the person
Gets help from someone you trust
items.why: These are four ways to step in that are kind and safe. Each does a different job, and a situation may need more than one.

items.p: A feeling that passes from one person to another, mostly without either choosing it, is called emotional ____.
items.why: Contagion means spreading. Giggles, yawns and fear can all spread between people, mostly without anyone choosing it.

items.p: In a fair test of hurry words, the bottle and the chana must change in every run.
items.why: False. In a fair test only one thing changes, which is what the helper says. The bottle, the chana and the hand height stay the same, so that any difference comes from the words.

items.p: People copy what they see others do in a place. What is 'what most people here do' called?
items.why: A social norm is what most people in a place do, or think they should do. A stress response is the body getting ready for action. A barrier stops people, and a charter is a list of agreed rules.

items.p: Sort each one. Is it a barrier, or does it remove a barrier?
items: a switch too high to reach
a notice with pictures as well as words
a wide door with a handrail
items.why: A barrier is anything that stops some people from using a place. A ramp, pictures and a wide door let more people in.

items.p: Friendly teasing that both people enjoy is bullying.
items.why: False. Bullying hurts, frightens or leaves out the same person again and again, and the person finds it hard to stop it. Friendly teasing is fun for both and stops when one says stop.

items.p: What does the stress response do to the body?
opts: Speeds the heart and tightens the muscles
Slows the heart and loosens the muscles
items.why: When something seems urgent or unsafe, the body gets ready for action. Adrenaline speeds the heart, breathing quickens and the muscles tighten.

items.p: Dignity of labour means that every honest ____ deserves equal respect.
items.why: Dignity of labour means every honest job deserves equal respect, including jobs that are poorly paid, such as cleaning.

items.p: A helper hurries a person who is dropping chana into a bottle. Explain why more chana might miss.
items.a: The hurry words make the body treat the moment as urgent. Adrenaline speeds the heart and tightens the muscles. Tight, quick hands aim less well.
items.why: A strong answer says that words from another person can start the stress response, and links tight muscles to poor aim.

items.p: Name two ways a place can teach a rule without any words. Say how each one works.
items.a: A clean wall tells people that litter is not done here, and a scribbled wall says the opposite. A line at a tap shows people to wait. People copy what they see others do.
items.why: A strong answer says that people read a place and copy what they see. It gives two real examples.

items.p: Draw a doorway that a person in a wheelchair and a person with a pram can both use. Label three features.
items.a: A wide doorway of at least 90 cm. A gentle ramp instead of a step, or no step. A low door handle and a low switch, between 40 and 120 cm from the floor.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a clear width of at least 90 cm and no step. It also shows that the controls are within reach of a seated person.
items.art: An empty rectangle for a doorway with three blank label lines beside it.

items.p: Who should clean a classroom at the end of the day?

views.says: The cleaner is paid to clean. Children should only keep the room tidy.
Children should share the cleaning in turn. Then they learn to respect the work.
Children can pick up their own things and greet me. I do the deep cleaning, and I need it to be safe.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For example: children should pick up their own things, because a mess is not only the cleaner's problem. But a child should not have to handle dirty or dangerous waste.
items.why: A strong answer uses an idea from the unit, such as dignity of labour, safety, or the way a place stays cared for. It treats the other views fairly.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, when someone shouts 'faster!' at you.
items: Hands feel tight and aim worse
Brain treats the moment as urgent
a: Brain treats the moment as urgent
Hands feel tight and aim worse
items.why: The brain first treats the words as urgent. The adrenal glands release adrenaline. The heart speeds up, and the muscles tighten, so hands aim less well.

items.p: A friend says someone is hurting her, and asks you to keep it secret. What should you do?
items.why: A secret about someone being hurt is too big for a child to carry. A trusted grown-up can get help. Telling is how your friend gets help.

worksheets.title: Why people copy, what barriers do, and how to step in

items.p: Riders dropped more paper beside scribbled walls than beside clean walls. What does this show?
opts: People copy what they see others do
items.why: A scribbled wall says that people here break rules, so more riders dropped paper. Nobody told them anything. The place gave the message.

items.p: Which is the kindest and safest first action when you see someone being teased?
opts: Say 'Stop, that is not funny' calmly
Join in so you are not next
items.why: A calm, short sentence can stop teasing without anyone being hurt. Joining in or pushing adds to the harm, and saying nothing gives the teaser an audience.

items.p: Why does one wrapper on the ground lead to more wrappers?
opts: People copy a sign that others have littered
items.why: A wrapper on the ground tells people that dropping wrappers is done here. A mess that others have left makes more mess likely.

items.p: Telling a grown-up about bullying is the same as telling tales.
items.why: False. Telling to get someone out of trouble is not the same as telling tales, which is done to get someone into trouble. Always tell when someone is being hurt.

items.p: A ramp that helps a person in a wheelchair can also help a person with a pram.
items.why: True. A change made for one person often helps many, such as a parent with a pram, a grandparent with a stick and a worker with a trolley.

items.p: Three of these help a big feeling settle. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Breathing out slowly, naming the feeling and talking to someone you trust all help a feeling settle. Keeping a big feeling secret for ever does not.

items.p: For each 1 cm of rise, a ramp needs 12 cm of length. A 15 cm step needs how many cm?
items.why: 15 times 12 is 180. So the ramp must be 180 cm long, which is 1.8 metres.

items.p: Sort each example. Does it show respect, or not?
items: cutting in while someone is speaking
waiting for your turn at the tap
laughing at the way someone speaks
dropping a wrapper that a worker must pick up
items.why: Respect means treating a person as someone who matters as much as you do. Each of the first kind of actions does that, and each of the others does not.

items.p: Match each example to the idea it shows.
pairs: One child giggles and the whole row giggles
The heart beats faster when someone shouts
Everyone takes off their shoes at a temple door
Hurting the same child again and again
items.why: Each example is a clear case of its idea. Contagion is a feeling spreading, and a norm is what most people do in a place.

items.p: Explain why a sign saying 'Many people drop litter here' can make litter worse.
items.a: The sign tells people that dropping litter is what most people do here. People copy what they see and read about others. A sign that asks people to keep the place clean works better.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sign sets a social norm in the wrong direction. It says that people follow what most others do.

items.p: Why does an audience keep bullying going? Say what a watcher can do instead.
items.a: An audience gives the bully attention, and laughing joins in. A watcher can say it calmly, stand beside the person, put it right or tell a grown-up. One child stepping in often stops it quickly.
items.why: A strong answer says that the watchers are part of it, and names at least two of the four ways to step in.

items.p: A ramp built for one wheelchair user helps other people too. Name three, and say why.
items.a: A parent with a pram, because wheels roll up a ramp. A grandparent with a stick, because a slope is easier than a step. A worker with a trolley, because a trolley cannot climb steps.
items.why: A strong answer names three groups and links each to a barrier that a ramp removes.

items.p: A school sees pushing at the water taps. What would work best?

views.says: Make a rule, and give a punishment to anyone who pushes.
Start a line yourself. The younger children will copy you.
Put in more taps, so that there is less to push about.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For example: a line started by older students works because people copy what they see, and it costs nothing. But more taps remove the reason to push. A rule alone may not work if people see others pushing.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that people copy what they see, or that the place makes the right action easy. It treats the other views fairly.

items.p: On a drawing of a doorway, label these four things: threshold, clear width, door handle, light switch.
a: Threshold: the raised edge on the floor
Clear width: the narrowest gap with the door open
Door handle: low enough for a seated person, between 40 and 120 cm
Light switch: also between 40 and 120 cm from the floor
items.why: These are the four things that decide whether a doorway can be used by a person in a wheelchair. A strong label says what each is and what a good size is.
items.art: An open doorway drawn from the front with a floor edge, a door open to one side, a handle and a switch on the wall, each with a blank label line.

items.p: Breathe ____ slowly, for longer than you breathe in, to help a big feeling settle.
items.why: A long out-breath slows the heart a little. The body can then settle sooner.

worksheets.title: Testing ideas about feelings, norms and kindness

items.p: A test finds that hurried hands miss more. How could you show that the words, not only the speed, caused it?
opts: Hurry yourself with no words, then compare
items.why: If the hand also misses more when it hurries itself in silence, the speed alone matters. If it misses more only with the hurry words, the words matter. Changing the bottle, the run count or the chana would not separate these.

items.p: A park sign says 'Most visitors take wood.' Which sign would work better?
opts: Please leave the wood where it is
items.why: A sign that says many people break a rule makes breaking it look normal. A simple, friendly request that shows the right action worked better in tests.

items.p: Cameras filmed real street quarrels, and someone helped in most. What does this suggest about crowds?
opts: Crowds do not always stop people helping
items.why: An old idea says that nobody helps when many are watching. Real films suggest that in most quarrels someone steps in. Scientists still argue about how well the old idea fits real life.

items.p: People are kind only because they are taught rules and given prizes.
items.why: False. Toddlers help others before anyone has taught them, and rats free trapped companions. Teaching and the community shape kindness, but they are not the only source.

items.p: Dignity of labour means every honest job must be paid exactly the same.
items.why: False. It means every honest job deserves equal respect. Pay is a separate question, which people argue about.

items.p: In the lane game, a roll of 1, 2 or 3 adds a wrapper. About how many of 60 rolls add one?
items.why: 3 of the 6 numbers add a wrapper, which is half. Half of 60 is 30.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair test in order.
items: Do each run and write the number
Decide what one thing to change
a: Decide what one thing to change
Do each run and write the number
items.why: A fair test starts with one thing to change. You keep the rest the same, run the test, and only then say what the numbers show.

items.p: A short list of rules that the people of a place agree on together and sign is called a ____.
items.why: A charter is agreed together and signed, so people feel it is theirs. Rules last longest when the people who use the place agree on them.

items.p: Telling people to form a line often fails, but standing in a line yourself often works. Explain why.
items.a: People copy what they see. A person shouting about a line is only words. A person standing in a line is a picture of what is done here, and others see that and join.
items.why: A strong answer says people follow what they see more than what they are told, and uses the idea of a social norm.

items.p: Is a narrow bathroom door a problem of the person who cannot get through, or of the building? Give evidence.
items.a: The building. The person cannot change the door by trying harder. A wider door would let every person through, so the door was made for people who walk.
items.why: A strong answer says a barrier is in the place, and gives a measurement or an example.

items.p: A classmate asks you to leave another child out. Write what you would say, and why.
items.a: 'I want to be friends with both of you.' A friend who asks you to leave someone out is asking for something unfair, and leaving the same person out again and again is a kind of bullying.
items.why: A strong answer is calm and short, and says why in terms of fairness or bullying.

items.p: Why might a calm voice and a smile help a hurried person do better work? Give two reasons from the body.
items.a: A calm voice does not start the stress response, so the heart stays slower and the muscles stay loose. A smile can be copied, so the other person's face and feelings relax too.
items.why: A strong answer names two body effects: the stress response and the copying of faces.

items.p: Is it fair that cleaning work is often paid the least?

views.says: Pay follows how many people can do a job, and many can do this one.
No place can run without this work, and it is risky. It should be paid well and made safe.
Whatever the pay, every honest job should be respected, and I should learn the names of the people who do it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For example: respect and pay are different questions. A place cannot run without cleaning, and the work protects everyone from illness, so that can be a reason to pay more. But pay is set by many things people disagree about.
items.why: A strong answer separates respect from pay, and uses a fact such as that a school with no cleaners would soon be unfit to use. It treats the other views fairly.

items.p: Draw a school water tap area where children stand in a line without being told. Label three features.
items.a: A line marked on the ground, a footprint or an arrow at each tap, a short row of taps so no one waits long, a shaded place to stand, and a notice with a picture.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the right action easy to see and easy to do, as in a line mark or a shorter wait.
items.art: An empty rectangle for a school yard with a row of taps at one side and three blank label lines.

items.p: Match each situation to the best first action.
pairs: Someone is being hurt and threatened
Tell a trusted grown-up at once
A classmate is left out of a game
Stand beside her and invite her
A classmate laughs at how someone reads aloud
items.why: Someone being hurt must always be told to a grown-up. The others can be put right by a child, calmly and kindly.

quiz.p: Which place is most likely to be a happy one?
opts: A plain room where people greet and help each other
A grand hall where people ignore each other
A new building where older children push
A big field with no rules
quiz.why: A happy place is made mostly by how the people in it treat each other. A plain room with kind people is happier than a fine one with unkind people.

quiz.p: One child starts to giggle and the whole row soon giggles. What is happening?
opts: A feeling is spreading from person to person
The row is learning a rule
quiz.why: This is emotional contagion. A feeling spreads through faces and voices, mostly without anyone choosing it.

quiz.p: Which substance enters the blood when the body gets ready for urgent action?
quiz.why: The two small adrenal glands above the kidneys release adrenaline. It speeds the heart within seconds.

quiz.p: Why does a fair test take turns between two kinds of run?
opts: So practice does not fool the result
quiz.why: If one kind came first, practice would help the later kind and the result would be unfair. Taking turns spreads the practice evenly.

quiz.p: Which shows respect for a person who cleans a school?
opts: Learn her name and greet her
Leave your rubbish on the floor
quiz.why: Respect means treating a person as someone who matters as much as you do. A greeting by name is a small, real act of it.

quiz.p: A door is 60 cm wide. Which person is most likely to be stopped?
opts: A person in a 65 cm wide wheelchair
A person with a school bag
quiz.why: A 65 cm wide chair cannot pass a 60 cm gap. A barrier is anything that stops some people from using a place.

quiz.p: A bigger child pushes a smaller child and says 'Tell anyone and you are next.' What is the best action?
opts: Tell a trusted grown-up at once
quiz.why: Someone is being hurt and threatened. A child should not step in alone. A trusted grown-up can make it stop.

quiz.p: Why is picking up the first wrapper better than picking up the tenth?
opts: Fewer wrappers mean fewer people copy
quiz.why: A mess feeds itself. With few wrappers few people add one, and with many wrappers most do. So the first wrapper matters most.

quiz.p: Which of these can help a big feeling settle?
opts: Breathing out slowly, longer than breathing in
quiz.why: A slow, long out-breath slows the heart a little. Naming the feeling, moving and talking to someone you trust also help.

applications: Schools put ramps, wide doors and low handrails on their buildings so that every child can get in. India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act of 2016 asks public buildings to be accessible.
Road signs use pictures and arrows, so that a driver who does not read the local language can still follow them.
A teacher who greets each child at the door, calmly and by name, sets the mood for the whole class before the lesson begins.
Many schools teach children four ways to step in when they see teasing: say it calmly, stand beside, put it right, or tell a grown-up.
Towns put bins close to where litter is dropped, and fix a broken lamp or a scribble quickly, because a place that is kept up stays kept up.
In 2013 India passed a law that bans employing people to clean dry toilets by hand. Campaigners such as Bezwada Wilson worked for decades to bring it about.
A family charter, signed by every member, helps a household agree on how to share a kitchen, a study corner or a lift.

open_questions.q: How much of kindness are we born with, and how much do we learn?
open_questions.why_open: Toddlers help before anyone teaches them, and children in different places share in different ways. Both facts are real, and nobody knows how to weigh them.

open_questions.q: When many people watch someone in trouble, do they help or hold back?
open_questions.why_open: An old test in 1968 found that people helped less when others were near. Films of real street quarrels in 2020 found that someone helped in most. Scientists are still working out why the two differ.

open_questions.q: Does copying a face create the feeling, or only show it?
open_questions.why_open: Face muscles copy faces within half a second. But in 2016 a large team tried to repeat a famous pen-in-the-mouth test and did not find the effect. How much a face changes a feeling is still being measured.

open_questions.q: How many people does it take to change what is normal in a place?
open_questions.why_open: In 2018 Damon Centola and his team found that when about a quarter of a group held to a new way of naming things, the whole group switched. Nobody knows whether real places and real habits work the same way.

open_questions.q: Do other animals feel for each other, or do they only act as if they do?
open_questions.why_open: Rats free trapped companions and elephants touch an upset elephant. Scientists disagree about what the helper feels, because nobody can ask them.

maths.problem: In made-up Hurry Test results, the three calm runs had 2, 1 and 3 misses. The three hurried runs had 5, 6 and 7. How many times as many misses did the hurried runs have?
maths.explain: Calm runs: 2 plus 1 plus 3 is 6. Hurried runs: 5 plus 6 plus 7 is 18. 18 divided by 6 is 3.
maths.context: In the Hurry Test you drop 15 chana into a bottle three times calmly and three times hurried. These are the made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Adding each kind of run first, and then dividing, shows how much more often the hurried runs missed.

maths.problem: In the made-up Hurry Test, the first calm run had a pulse of 21 beats in 15 seconds. The first hurried run had 23. How many more beats in a minute was that?
maths.explain: A minute is 4 times 15 seconds. 21 times 4 is 84, and 23 times 4 is 92. 92 take away 84 is 8.
maths.context: In the Hurry Test you count your pulse for 15 seconds after each run. These are the first two made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A count for 15 seconds is hard to compare with the pulse you know. Multiplying by 4 gives beats in a minute.

maths.problem: In the made-up Smile Count, 6 of 10 people smiled back at a smile, and 2 of 10 at a plain face. What percentage of each group smiled back? How many times as likely was a smile to be returned?
maths.answer: 60 out of 100 and 20 out of 100, so 3 times as likely.
maths.explain: 6 out of 10 is 60 out of 100, which is 60 percent. 2 out of 10 is 20 percent. 60 divided by 20 is 3.
maths.context: In the Smile Count you greet 10 people with a smile and 10 with a plain face. These are the made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Turning each count into a percentage lets you compare two groups, even if the groups are different sizes.

maths.problem: In the made-up Doorway Test, the bathroom door was 64 cm wide. A common wheelchair is 65 cm wide, and guides ask for 90 cm. By how many cm is the door too narrow for the chair? By how many cm is it short of the guide?
maths.answer: 1 cm too narrow for the chair, and 26 cm short of the guide.
maths.explain: 65 take away 64 is 1. 90 take away 64 is 26.
maths.context: In the Doorway Test you measure doors against a 65 cm string and a 90 cm string. This is a made-up bathroom door.
maths.why_maths: A difference in centimetres shows how big a change a builder would need to make.

maths.problem: A ramp needs 12 cm of length for each 1 cm of rise. A step at a library door is 15 cm high. How long must the ramp be, in metres?
maths.explain: 15 times 12 is 180 centimetres. 100 centimetres make a metre, so 180 centimetres is 1.8 metres.
maths.context: In The Ramp That Fits you plan a ramp for a 15 cm step, and you build it as a model. 1 cm in the model stands for 10 cm in real life.
maths.why_maths: The rule of 12 for each 1 gives the real length, and the model shows it is 18 cm, which is a tenth as long.

maths.problem: A 90 cm ramp rises 7.5 cm. A guide asks for 12 cm of length for each 1 cm of rise. Does the ramp meet the guide?
maths.answer: Yes, just. It has exactly 12 cm of length for each 1 cm of rise.
maths.explain: 90 divided by 7.5 is 12. The guide asks for 12 or more, so the ramp meets it exactly.
maths.context: In The Ramp That Fits you work out how many centimetres of ramp you have for each 1 cm of rise.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the length by the rise gives one number that you can check against the guide.

maths.problem: In Keep the Lane Clean, with 2 wrappers in the lane a passer-by adds one when the die shows 1 or 2. With 4 wrappers, it shows 1 to 4. Out of 30 passers-by, how many would add a wrapper in each lane?
maths.answer: About 10 in the first lane and about 20 in the second.
maths.explain: With 2 wrappers, 2 of the 6 numbers add one, which is a third. A third of 30 is 10. With 4 wrappers, 4 of 6 is two thirds. Two thirds of 30 is 20.
maths.context: In the game Keep the Lane Clean you roll a die for each passer-by. The more wrappers in the lane, the more numbers on the die add another.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the die faces gives the chance that a passer-by copies the mess. It shows why an early pick-up matters.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how psychologists found out that children copy what they see, even when nobody rewards them. It overturned an idea that many teachers had held.
how_we_found_out.story: Until the 1960s, many psychologists taught that a child learns a behaviour only when she is rewarded or punished for it. Copying, they said, mattered little. In 1961 Albert Bandura and his colleagues Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross tested this at a nursery school at Stanford University in California. They watched 72 children aged 3 to 6. One group saw a grown-up hit and shout at a big inflatable doll. A second group saw a grown-up play quietly with toys. A third group saw no grown-up at all. Then each child was left in a room with the same doll and toys. Nobody rewarded or praised any child. Yet the children who had watched the hitting hit the doll far more, and some used the same words and movements. Later work showed that children also notice whether the grown-up is praised or punished. But a child's learning could no longer be explained by her own rewards alone.
how_we_found_out.who: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross at Stanford University, California
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That children learn only from what they are rewarded or punished for themselves. In Bandura's test, children copied a grown-up's actions and words with no reward at all.
how_we_found_out.art: A nursery room with a big inflatable doll in one corner, toys on a low table, and a small group of children watching through a window as a grown-up plays quietly with blocks.

roots.context: In the Hurry Test and the Smile Count, another person's words and face changed what your own body did. Here we ask what this tells us about where a skill, a mood and a place really come from.

deep_truth.truth: In the Hurry Test, the same hand and the same chana did worse when someone said 'faster'. The words entered through the ears and reached the heart and the fingers within seconds. In the Smile Count, one face moved another face. So a skill or a mood is never made inside one person alone.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'she is careful' or 'he is clumsy', as if a skill sat inside one person like a coin in a pocket. Yet each body is being changed all the time by the faces, voices and actions of the people near it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hurry Test the helper changes only the words, and many people then miss more and have a quicker pulse. In 2000, Ulf Dimberg's sensors showed face muscles copying a face within half a second. In the Smile Count you see how often a smile is returned.

three.who_am_i: You are partly made by the people around you. Your face, your voice and your aim all change with who is in the room.
three.what_is_life: Living beings change each other's bodies all the time. Rats free trapped companions, elephants comfort an upset elephant, and a toddler hands back a dropped peg.
three.what_is_this_world: A place is made of the people in it. Its mood and its rules pass from one person to the next, so no place stands apart from the people who use it.

roots.thread: A mood, a habit or a skill passes from one body to another through faces, voices and actions. A giggling row, a line at a tap and a quiet room are each one shared state held by many people. Many sages taught that all beings share one awareness, even though each of us looks out from a different body. This unit shows one small, measurable case of it. The state of a place is held by all of its people together.

teachings.teaching: In Indra's net, a bright jewel hangs at every knot, and each jewel shows the reflection of all the others.
teachings.link: A face in a room shows the faces around it. A smile or a frown is reflected from one person to the next. The sutra is a picture from a Buddhist text, and the unit's measurements stand without it.

teachings.source: Ubuntu, a saying of the Zulu and Xhosa peoples of southern Africa: 'umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu'
teachings.teaching: A person is a person through other persons.
teachings.link: The Hurry Test shows one exact case. A person's aim, pulse and mood are shaped by what other people say and do near them.

teachings.teaching: Share your food and look after all living beings. The wise count this as the first of all duties.
teachings.link: A place where people share and care for each other and for the place is a happy place. The unit shows how such habits pass from person to person, as a line at a tap passes from three people to many.

science.text: Seeing a face makes your own face muscles begin to copy it, often within half a second, even when you do not notice the face.
Whether copying a face creates the feeling itself, or only goes along with it, is still being measured. Some famous tests could not be repeated.

other_view.view: People differ from the start in how easily they feel stress, and in how steady their hands are. A skill belongs to a person, and a place adds only a little to it. Both views have evidence. How much comes from the person and how much from the people around is still being measured.

practice.title: Passing on a calm face
practice.say: Sit facing your child. Look at each other's faces for a few breaths. Breathe out slowly and let your face rest. Notice whether the other face changes. Then each of you picks one person you will meet tomorrow who will get a calm face from you.
practice.kid: Sit facing a grown-up. Breathe out slowly. Let your face rest. Does their face change too?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. The Hurry Test (core) needs only a plastic bottle, a plate, 15 chana and a helper. A 1-litre bottle with a 30 cm drop gives about 1 to 3 misses in a calm round, and the step says how to change the height or the bottle if it gives none or too many. A few families will see no difference between calm and hurried runs, and the step says that this is a real result. The test cannot separate the hurry words from the hurry itself, and the last step asks the child how it could. The Smile Count needs a place where about 20 people pass in 20 minutes, with a grown-up beside the child. In a quiet building it may need two days. A city crowd may return fewer smiles, so the unit asks the child to compare within their own count. The Doorway Test needs only a tape measure or a ruler, two pieces of string and a few pencil marks. Most homes will find at least one door or edge that stops a 65 cm wheelchair. The Ramp That Fits uses card and a notebook as a 1 to 10 model, and its numbers were checked: a 12 cm ramp rises 1.5 cm at 1 in 8, which is too steep, and an 18 cm ramp that runs sideways along the step fits in the 12 cm of ground at 1 in 12. Keep the Lane Clean was simulated 100,000 times. With 2 wrappers and early pick-ups it is won about 9 times in 10. With 4 wrappers it is won about 1 time in 4, even with the best play. What Helped? is a small log, and pulse differences of a few beats are normal, so the step says one trial is not enough. Nothing in this unit diagnoses or treats a feeling, and each time a feeling is too big the child is told to tell a trusted grown-up. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the 90 cm door, the 1 in 12 slope, the 120 cm ramp width, the 150 cm landing and the 40 to 120 cm reach range against India's 2016 Harmonised Guidelines (the reach range is rounded from 38 to 120 cm); the 65 cm wheelchair is a round figure for chairs of about 60 to 70 cm; the study details, years, counts and the Tirukkural number were checked; the ramp width was corrected from 90 to 120 cm, and the figures for bathroom edges, door widths and switch heights were removed. The Ubuntu and Indra's net teachings are paraphrased. The three videos have no address yet.
